Introduction:

Music streaming services are constantly changing the way their listeners discover new artists through the use of machine-learning recommendation systems that curate an experience that aligns with a specific user’s taste. Whether it’s Spotify deploying a new weekly playlist or Apple Music recommending similar artists, machine-learning models must learn to understand what makes a song belong to a particular genre. In doing so, insights about what music garners the most attention can be properly generated in real-time. Here, supervised learning seeks to allow streaming services to predict a song’s genre using audio and lyrical features that are present within metadata. This process reveals the elements of the music that are important enough for mass appeal (Recommendation). I decided to apply this technique to a dataset of songs from many different decades to help determine a song’s genre using a mix of audio signal characteristics (e.g., acousticness, loudness, energy) and content-based features (e.g., romantic, obscene, sadness, dating). The finalized model utilized random forest classification due to the categorical nature of the endeavor, and it was able to achieve an accuracy of 41 % with the data that it was initially trained on. Although this was far from the ideal amount of accuracy that I sought to have, the model still uncovered valuable information about genre patterns and genre classification limitations in the current age of music.

Research Question:

How can musical genres be accurately mapped and predicted using certain audio and lyrical features for listeners to enjoy?

Stakeholders:

Music streaming platforms like Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube Music, and Amazon Music all have a need for user engagement on their platform, and this analysis would certainly help them with that. As new music keeps releasing every week and the demand for the next hit song increases, executives and marketing teams at these corporations will become more interested in improving how they recommend new artists and generate playlists automatically. This is especially true in situations where metadata for a song might be incomplete, or when different songs are grouped together by similarity. The complexity of the scenario further arises when music begins to get mislabeled or remains unlabeled after production. The current state of music has evolved into an amalgamation of many different genres and sub-genres, which makes it very easy for tracks to be uploaded without the selection of the correct genres that perfectly encapsulate their essence. Furthermore, the metadata that is used in its classification may vary across different record labels and eras in which the song came out (Inconsistent). As a result, it is very important for music directors at these companies to have a machine-learning model that has a good understanding of what makes a song a certain genre.

Decisions:

The development of a supervised model that can accurately detect the genre from song characteristics will allow music platforms to begin making choices that help their services to be more reliable for their users. Whether they are a casual or heavy music listener, this approach seeks to make the experience better for all. For instance, a service like Spotify might decide to generate audio tags for specific genres on tracks that don’t have good metadata, providing aid for those who may’ve been confused about what they were listening to. In addition, the ability of this learning model to work based on the data that it receives will help services like Apple Music improve similarity-based recommendations in the future, since the genres that are assigned to a song will be more precise. This functionality can be paired with a commitment to flagging songs whose genres appear to be mislabeled so that the listeners can actually discover songs that are more aligned with their general preferences.

Data:

This data was pulled from Kaggle, and it contains lyrics and metadata for songs that were obtained through APIs. According to the NIAID Data Discovery Portal, “the audio data was scraped using Echo Nest® API integrated engine with spotipy Python’s package. The spotipy API permits the user to search for specific genres, artists, songs, release date, etc. To obtain the lyrics we used the Lyrics Genius® API as baseURL for requesting data based on the song title and artist name”. Furthermore, the lyrical themes have been processed to display scores on themes from 0 to 1, and then are manipulated by me for a deeper picture to be unveiled in the supervised learning. With 28,372 rows and 31 columns, it represents song lyrical content labels (thematic intensity) and audio features (numeric) from multiple decades (1950–2019).

The fields are as follows:

artist_name (5,426 unique values, 28,372 total): The name of the artist or group who performed the song (STRING).

track_name (23,689 unique values, 28,372 total): The name of the song (STRING).

release_date (1950–2019, 28,372 total values): The year the song was released (INTEGER).

genre (7 unique values, 28,372 total): The musical genre category for the song (STRING).

lyrics (28,372 unique values): The raw text of the song’s lyrics (STRING).

len (28,372 unique values): The number of words in the lyrics (INTEGER).

dating (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to the themes of romance, courtship, and relationships (FLOAT).

violence (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of aggression, conflict, and physical force (FLOAT).

world/life (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of society, existence, and philosophical thought (FLOAT).

night/time (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of nighttime, the passage of time, and moments (FLOAT).

shake the audience (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of impact, excitement, and energizing the listener (FLOAT).

family/gospel (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of family, spirituality, and religion (FLOAT).

romantic (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of love, passion, and intimacy (FLOAT).

communication (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of talking, expression, and dialogue (FLOAT).

obscene (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of profanity, vulgarity, and explicit content (FLOAT).

music (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to meta-themes about music itself, instruments, or sound (FLOAT).

movement/places (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of travel, location, and motion (FLOAT).

light/visual perceptions (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of sight, illumination, and imagery (FLOAT).

family/spiritual (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of kinship and faith (FLOAT).

like/girls (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of attraction, liking, and often, specifically, women (FLOAT).

sadness (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of sorrow, heartbreak, and melancholy (FLOAT).

feelings (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of emotions, sensitivity, and affect (FLOAT).

danceability (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of dancing, rhythm, and movement (FLOAT).

loudness (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1. Likely derived from lyrics referencing volume, noise, or intensity (FLOAT).

acousticness (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1. Likely derived from lyrics referencing organic, non-electric, or soft sounds (FLOAT).

instrumentalness (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1. Likely derived from lyrics referencing instruments or music without words (FLOAT).

valence (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s positiveness. High valence sounds more positive (e.g., happy, cheerful, euphoric), while low valence sounds more negative (FLOAT).

energy (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s intensity and activity. High energy feels fast, loud, and noisy (FLOAT).

topic (28,372 unique values): A categorical label assigning the song’s main theme based on the highest scoring theme field (STRING).

age (28,372 unique values): A normalized score (0–1) representing the release date, where 1.0 is the oldest (1950), and 0.0 is the newest (2019) in the dataset (FLOAT).

To predict genre, two categories of feature columns were relied upon:

  1. Audio features (numeric, continuous):
  • Danceability
  • Loudness
  • Acousticness
  • Instrumentalness
  • Energy
  • Valence

These relate to the “feel” of a song and are modeled after Spotify’s audio features.

2. Lyrical sentiment/context Features (numeric, continuous):

  • Romantic
  • Violence
  • Obscene
  • Dating
  • Sadness

These reflect language usage in lyrics and attempt to quantify emotional or thematic content.

Ground-Truth Labels:

The supervised labels from the dataset’s genre field, with some represented better than others:

  • Pop
  • Rock
  • Jazz
  • Hip hop
  • Country
  • Reggae
  • Blues

These labels serve as the supervised ground truth, assigned based on metadata sources from music databases and catalog labels.

Methods and Course Concepts Applied:

This project builds directly on multiple methodological frameworks covered throughout the course, successfully integrating both supervised and unsupervised learning techniques to analyze and predict music genres. I wanted to get a level of predictive accuracy that made sense for the data, potentially helping to understand why certain genres might be more difficult to distinguish based on audio and lyrical features present in my feature columns. To achieve this, methods from the supervised learning (module 6), model evaluation (module 7), and clustering (module 4) modules were applied.

The supervised learning methods made up the core of this project, as it relied on supervised classification, which trained models using genre label data. I was able to use it to learn relationships between numerical features (danceability, energy, and lyrical sentiment indicators) and categorical genre labels. The random forest classifier was used as the baseline supervised model, which built an ensemble of decision trees trained on random subsets of the data and features before aggregating the predictions through majority voting. Random forests are well-suited for tabular data and can detect nonlinear relationships between features without strong parametric assumptions. In this scenario, they provided a strong initial benchmark that allowed me to extract feature importance scores and get interpretability into musical and lyrical features that most influenced genre predictions overall. The gradient boosting classifier was meant to build on this random forest approach by utilizing the decision trees sequentially so that each new tree focused on correcting the errors made by previous trees. This method emphasizes difficult to classify observations and often performs well when class boundaries are complex or overlapping. Applying gradient boosting allowed for a comparison between different strategies and provided insight into how error-focused learning affects genre classification performances. When paired together, these supervised learning methods reflect concepts from the supervised learning module, including classification and model generalizations.

The model evaluation techniques were critical for understanding the model’s performance beyond a single accuracy metric. The project applies several evaluation techniques covered in the model evaluation module to assess how well the classifiers perform across different genres (multi-classification). Train-test splitting was utilized to split the dataset into training and testing subsets using a stratified approach to preserve the genre distribution. This ensured that evaluation results reflected performance on unseen data rather than memorized training examples. The overall accuracy was used as a high-level performance metric, measuring the proportion of correctly classified songs. Although its output was useful for quick and easy comparisons to be drawn across models, the accuracy alone does not capture genre class-specific performance. The classification reports provided a more nuanced evaluation showcasing precision, recall, F1-score, and support, which could be computed for each genre. Together, these metrics revealed whether certain genres were systematically over- or under-predicted and helped identify imbalanced or ambiguous genres. Confusion matrices helped to visualize prediction errors across genres by examining which genres were most frequently misunderstood by the models. The analysis revealed meaningful patterns such as overlap between pop, rock, and blues, aligning with real-world musical similarities. This evaluation method directly supports interpretability and error analysis.

The clustering and unsupervised learning analysis present in the project incorporates methods that explore the underlying structure of the data without relying too much on genre labels. For instance, K-Means clustering was applied to standardized feature data to group songs based solely on their audio and lyrical characteristics. The number of clusters was set equal to the number of genres, enabling a direct comparison between unsupervised clusters and known genre labels. This analysis helped determine whether genres naturally form distinct groups in feature space or exhibit significant overlap. Since K-Means is Euclidean distance-based, all features were standardized using z-score normalization to ensure that no single feature dominates the clustering process due to scale differences. In order to visualize the high-dimensional feature space, PCA was included to reduce the data to two principal components. PCA preserves the directions of greatest variance and allows for a two-dimensional visualization of song similarity (despite the original high-dimensionality of the song features). By having genre labels alongside cluster assignments on the PCA scatterplot, the analysis was able to reveal substantial genre overlap and explain why supervised models struggle with certain genre distributions (through another lens).

The integration of supervised classification, model evaluation, and unsupervised clustering in this project demonstrates how multiple course modules can be put into a cohesive outcome. The supervised models quantify predictions, evaluation metrics diagnose the model strengths and weaknesses, and clustering analysis provides structural insights into genre ambiguity. Together, these module methods reinforce the idea that music genre prediction is not a strictly separable classification task, but rather shaped by overlapping musical and lyrical characteristics.

Exploratory Data Analysis (Supervised Learning):

Conducted in a Python Jupyter Notebook environment using pandas, numpy, sklearn, matplotlib, and seaborn.

The need to categorize genres based on the given information from the dataset called for the utilization of a multi-classification supervised learning environment, as genre is a categorical variable (hip hop, jazz, reggae, etc.). With 7 possible classes, the data was non-numeric, and regression would in no way be appropriate.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, confusion_matrix, accuracy_score
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# data loaded

df = pd.read_csv("tcc_ceds_music.csv")


print(f"Shape of Data: {df.shape}")  # rows/columns

# missing values check

print("Missing values:")
print(
    df[["genre", "danceability", "energy", "valence"]].isnull().sum()
)  # counting and summing up empty/missing areas

# genres for classification

major_genres = ["pop", "rock", "jazz", "hip hop", "country", "reggae", "blues"]
df_2 = df[df["genre"].isin(major_genres)].copy()  # new data frame to manipulate

# features used to predict genre of a song

feature_columns = [
    "danceability",
    "loudness",
    "acousticness",
    "instrumentalness",
    "valence",
    "energy",
    "dating",
    "violence",
    "romantic",
    "obscene",
    "sadness",
]

input = df_2[
    feature_columns
]  # storing features for input that the model can learn from
output = df_2["genre"]  # target labeling info that the model must predict

# splitting the data for 80/20 train/test compilation

input_train, input_test, output_train, output_test = train_test_split(
    input, output, test_size=0.2, stratify=output
)

# training model

rf_model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100)
rf_model.fit(
    input_train, output_train
)  # fit the random forest model to the training data so that it can learn patterns

This code showcases my initial approach to this multi-classification problem after loading the data and confirming that there were no missing values, then creating a new data frame that contained all the genres I wanted to examine. After creating this copy, I selected 11 total features that would help my model learn numeric patterns from the 0–1 scale that was given to measure them. By blending audio characteristics and lyrical sentiment, I could see a balanced picture that conceptually tied into the genre. For example, Jazz tends to have high instrumentalness throughout the record, while hip hop delves into high obscenity or violence scores. On the other hand, pop tends to be high in danceability and valence, while the blues are high in sadness and romance. After defining the features that the model was to learn from, I specified what it was supposed to be predicting (genres) so that the data could be split into an 80% training set and a 20% testing set that stratified the result by genre. In doing this, I could preserve a distribution that best represented the entire population in an unbiased and generalizable way, despite the imbalanced data that had a large number of songs in some genres but not others (e.g., 7042 songs vs 904 hip hop songs). I used a random forest classification model since the genre-feature relationship I was creating worked with non-linear connections. This would also mean that noise and irrelevant variables could be handled better before the production of feature importance metrics that are critical for creating insights. The random forest model performs well with mixed-scale numeric variables, so no feature standardization was required. Even though this dataset had 7 genres whose features could vary at any given point in time, the use of multiple decision trees (100) circumvented this issue well.

Classification Report 1:

# predict genre
output_prediction = rf_model.predict(input_test) # begins predicting genre for input set of feature columns 

# accuracy score
accuracy = accuracy_score(output_test, output_prediction) # compares predictions for genre with what genre labels for each song actually were 
print(f"Model Accuracy: {accuracy:.2f}")
print("Classification Report:")
print(classification_report(output_test, output_prediction)) # showcasing performance metrics for each genre analyzed

"""
Precision: How many predicted as X were actually X (Reliability)
Recall: How many actual X were correctly predicted as X (Validity)
F1-Score: Balance between precision and recall
Support: Number of samples for each genre 
"""

Model Accuracy: 0.41
Classification Report:
              precision    recall  f1-score   support

       blues       0.35      0.30      0.32       921
     country       0.42      0.54      0.47      1089
     hip hop       0.55      0.43      0.48       181
        jazz       0.48      0.37      0.42       769
         pop       0.37      0.43      0.40      1408
      reggae       0.48      0.47      0.48       500
        rock       0.44      0.33      0.37       807

    accuracy                           0.41      5675
   macro avg       0.44      0.41      0.42      5675
weighted avg       0.42      0.41      0.41      5675

This code block reveals how genres were predicted from the input of each feature column before the assignment of an accuracy score and a classification report. The accuracy rating of 41% was lower than expected, but it still made sense for the given data that had 7 genres with many overlapping characteristics that could easily be misinterpreted by the model. It’s also likely that the lower rating was exacerbated by the sheer amount of imbalance in data representation that existed among the genres. This could easily happen despite my best efforts to contain it. Regardless, the model fares 3 times better than the base chance one would have off simply predicting what genre the song is using observations alone, since the ratio for that scenario would be 1/7 (yielding a 14% chance of guessing right on each attempt). The classification report told a vivid story about how each genre actually performed in the model, utilizing precision, recall, f1-score, and support as measurements. Precision represents the percentage metric that shows songs predicted as genre X that actually were genre X, while recall takes the songs that actually were genre X and displays what percentage were correctly predicted (Ratio flipped). The f1-score extracts the harmonic mean of precision and recall together to showcase the balance that exists between them. Support simply represented the number of samples being used for each of these genres. Genres like hip-hop performed quite well, with a precision score of 0.55 and a recall score of 0.43. This meant that whenever the model predicted that a song was hip hop, it was right 55% of the time and found 43% of hip hop songs in total, as hip hop has distinctive features that make it a bit easier to identify. Genres like the blues did poorly with a precision score of 0.35 and a recall score of 0.30, meaning that 70% of blues records were missed and only 35% of actual predictions were correct within the 30% that were analyzed. However, this makes sense, since blues as a genre is often emulated and used as inspiration for the creation of music in many other genres that are present in the dataset. As a result, it is quite easy for the model to miss out on certain portions of the musical landscape that are heavily influenced by soulful music (Share a lot of similar audio features).

Plot 1:

# confusion matrix heatmap to display correct and incorrect predictions 
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 8))
heatmap_cm = confusion_matrix(output_test, output_prediction) # predictions on the diagonal are correct, but predictions off of the diagonal are incorrect errors
sns.heatmap(heatmap_cm, annot=True, fmt='d', cmap='YlOrRd', # display numbers as integers (no floating point values) with color scheming
            xticklabels=rf_model.classes_, 
            yticklabels=rf_model.classes_) # tick mark labeling corresponding to genres (classes)
plt.title('Genre Classification Confusion Matrix')
plt.xlabel('Predicted Genre')
plt.ylabel('True Genre')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

This code assists in generating a confusion matrix heatmap that isolates correct prediction scores numerically on the matrix diagonal, and incorrect error prediction values for any numbers that reside off the diagonal. In providing valid labeling for each tick mark, it becomes clear to see that pop and country were the most correctly predicted genres out of the 7 that were present. Most genres on the diagonal were about in the middle for prediction accuracy, with hip hop being the only outlier due to class imbalance (Hip hop only has 181 samples, while pop and country have over 1000), and genre ambiguity issues (Feature overlap). Hints of genre misclassifications existed between the pop-country pairs, pop-rock pairs, blues-country pairs, and blues-pop pairs. However, this is likely due to the lack of granularity and genre distinctions for audios that are sonically similar to one another. Regardless, the outcome of this confusion matrix is still within reason, since the borders between each genre are blurry. Musical features alone don’t strictly enforce categorical boundaries, so the presence of mistakes in some areas makes perfect sense.

Plot 2:

# horizontal bar chart to see how much importance each feature had in calculation
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
feature_importance = pd.DataFrame({ # creating dataframe for storage 
    'feature': feature_columns, # names for each feature 
    'importance': rf_model.feature_importances_ # ranking model's feature importance with scoring (sums up to be 1.0 in total) 
}).sort_values('importance', ascending=True)

colors = ['#FF6B6B', '#4ECDC4', '#45B7D1', '#96CEB4', '#FECA57', 
          '#FF9FF3', '#54A0FF', '#5F27CD', '#00D2D3', '#FF9F43', '#10AC84']

plt.barh(feature_importance['feature'], feature_importance['importance'], color = colors, linewidth = 0.5, edgecolor = 'black') # Y - X mapping for variables (horizontal)
plt.title('Feature Importance - Random Forest Classifier')
plt.xlabel('Importance Score')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

This code block generates a horizontal bar chart using a dataframe that ranks the machine-learning model’s feature importance for each attribute. After sorting the chart to hold each bar in the valid order and assigning a score of importance that is visibly distinguished by color, I was able to definitively see the values for each feature. Out of the 11 features that were present for analysis, danceability, acousticness, energy, instrumentalness, and valence were deemed to be the top 5 most important, with scores around 0.08 model contribution or higher. This meant that each one of these features influenced 8% or more of the model’s decisions for genre prediction. Altogether, these 11 add up to account for 100% of the model’s decision-making process. The lack of prevalent scores toward the lower end of the graph likely explains why some genres don’t get accurately analyzed by the model. Sometimes this could be attributed to less support from the training data (samples). Despite all of this, the outcome is still within intuitive expectations.

  • Danceability distinguishes pop from jazz, blues, and rock
  • Acousticness helps identify folk-influenced genres like country
  • Energy separates hip hop and rock from jazz
  • Instrumentalness is critical for traditional jazz and modern instrumental jazz
  • Valence distinguishes darker-toned genres from upbeat ones

The least influential features ended up being dating, romance, sadness, obscenity, and violence, indicating that lyrical content contributes to genre predictions less than audio features. This sort of information is extremely valuable in the development of recommendation systems for said music throughout various streaming services.

Misclassifications:

# indices of the test set to link back to original data

test_indices = input_test.index  # original row indices from df_2

# results DataFrame (actual vs predicted)

detailed_results = pd.DataFrame({
    'actual_genre': output_test, # true genre labels 
    'predicted_genre': output_prediction, # model predictions 
    'is_correct': (output_test == output_prediction) # true if correct, false if wrong
}, index=test_indices)

# assign song detail columns for analysis (if available for each song)

available_columns = [col for col in ['artist_name', 'track_name', 'release_date', 'lyrics'] if col in df_2.columns]
print(f"Available song detail columns: {available_columns}")

if available_columns: # getting song details from dataset

    song_details = df_2[available_columns]

    # merging song details with model's genre prediction results

    detailed_results = detailed_results.merge(
        song_details, 
        left_index=True, # index from left DataFrame (detailed_results)
        right_index=True, # index from right DataFrame (song_details)
        suffixes=('', '_original') # suffix for overlapping column names 
    )

    # getting misclassified songs

    misclassified_songs = detailed_results[~detailed_results['is_correct']]

    print(f"\nTotal misclassified songs: {len(misclassified_songs)}")
    print(f"Misclassification rate: {len(misclassified_songs)/len(input_test):.2%}")

    # top misclassified songs

    print("\nTop 15 Misclassified Songs:")


    for song_number, (index, row) in enumerate(misclassified_songs.head(15).iterrows()):
        print(f"{song_number+1:2d}. ", end="")

        if 'artist_name' in row:
            artist = str(row['artist_name'])[:25]  # truncate to 25 characters
            print(f"Artist: {artist:<25}", end="") # new line with left-aligned padding to 25 width for each artist (proper spacing) 

        if 'track_name' in row:
            track = str(row['track_name'])[:35]  # truncate to 35 characters
            print(f"Track: {track:<35}", end="") # new line with left-aligned padding to 35 width for each track (better space)


        print(f"Actual: {row['actual_genre']:>8} --> Predicted: {row['predicted_genre']:>8}") # right-aligned padding to 8 width for better spacing in output

        # key 'audio' features that might explain the misclassification

        if index in input_test.index: # if index exists get the values/features of that song index and print them
            song_features = input_test.loc[index]
            print(f"     Features - Dance: {song_features['danceability']:.2f}, "
                  f"Energy: {song_features['energy']:.2f}, "
                  f"Acoustic: {song_features['acousticness']:.2f}, "
                  f"Valence: {song_features['valence']:.2f}")
        print("\n")

    # most common misclassification patterns (commonly confused with one another)

    print("\nMost Common Misclassification Patterns:")

    confusion_patterns = pd.crosstab(misclassified_songs['actual_genre'], 
                                   misclassified_songs['predicted_genre'])
    print(confusion_patterns) # cross tabulation frequency table (matrix) being produced to show number of songs actually apart of a certain genre being predicted as such
    # actual vs predicted
    # genres most confused by model

    print("\nTop Genre Confusion Pairs:")

    confusion_pairs = [] # empty list to store the confused genre pairs 
    for actual_genre in confusion_patterns.index:
        for predicted_genre in confusion_patterns.columns:
            if actual_genre != predicted_genre: # for genres in nested loop, if actual genre doesn't equal predicted genre, assign the result to a count and append the outcome as a flawed pair
                count = confusion_patterns.loc[actual_genre, predicted_genre] # getting value at the intersection of predicted genre rows and actual genre columns to see how many were misclassified 
                confusion_pairs.append((actual_genre, predicted_genre, count))

    # sorting by frequency (count -- 3rd element of list) and showing top 5 confusion pairs in descending order

    confusion_pairs.sort(key=lambda x: x[2], reverse=True)
    for number, (actual, predicted, count) in enumerate(confusion_pairs[:5]):
        print(f"{number+1}. {actual} --> {predicted}: {count} songs")

else: # if some details weren't present print that and showcase what is present in dataframe
    print("No song detail columns found in the dataset.")
    print("Available columns:", df_2.columns.tolist())

This code block showcases my approach to listing a few songs that were misclassified alongside the patterns that emerged from their misclassification on a broad scale. In linking the indices of the test set of data for the model back to the original data that held the song information, I was able to create and merge a data frame full of the model’s genre prediction results with song details (provided that they were initially available/existed). From here, I noted the number of songs that were misclassified and came out with a rate of around 59%. This made sense, as the accuracy rating for the original model came out to be around 41%, allowing for the full capabilities of prediction to be verified since 100–41 = 59 (100% in total). After iterating through the top 15 misclassified songs with consistent formatting for the output, I decided to include the values of audio features that each of these distinct songs had, so that an explanation for their misclassification could be uncovered. The actual vs predicted genre frequency table (matrix) was created with this same goal in mind, and the top 5 pairs of genres that the model got confused were sorted through efficiently.

  1. Pop ←→ Country

Pop songs incorrectly labeled as country records (And vice-versa) consistently occurred as an issue in the model’s predictions, as these two genres held the highest amount of representation within the data out of the 7 present. They also crossover a lot in modern music to produce records with high acousticness, danceability, and sentimental lyrical themes. Without a reliable means of delineating instrumentation beyond the feature rating given in the data, the machine-learning model likely can’t differentiate between the two genres well enough for accuracy purposes. Pop songs like Post Malone’s “Blame It on Me” were predicted to be country due to its high danceability, energy, and lyrics, while country songs like Blake Shelton’s “Home” were predicted to be pop due to its balanced acoustic nature.

2. Rock → Pop

Rock songs being predicted as pop were common misclassifications due to the soft, melodic, or acoustic sounds from rock music that can often structurally resemble pop music on many different levels. From varying levels of volume and energy to high amounts of valence, the room for mistakes with a machine-learning model that can’t necessarily distinguish actual sounds in the music is high. U2’s rock song “God Part II” was incorrectly assessed as a pop song due to its high level of valence and energy that one could also dance to, while Imagine Dragons’ rock song “Yesterday” was predicted to be pop music because it was well-rounded in these same areas.

3. Blues ←→ Pop

Blues songs being predicted as pop (And vice-versa) happened at a surprisingly high rate due to the level of influence blues has as a genre that the machine-learning model isn’t able to distinguish without historical context. Pop music as a whole evolved and continues to develop from blues/r&b roots with many similar chord progressions. Emotional and soulful singing often appears in both as a result of this reality, with singers like Adele being placed in the pop genre despite their sound being curated by traditional Black blues artists. Blues songs like The Animals’ “Many Rivers to Cross” and Joe Cocker’s “I Stand in Wonder” were incorrectly predicted as pop songs for this exact reason. As perfect examples of this occurrence, “Many Rivers to Cross” is originally a song that comes from the Black reggae artist Jimmy Cliff, and Joe Cocker was heavily influenced by the soulful music Black Americans made in the '60s and '70s.

4. Blues ←→ Country

Blues songs being incorrectly labeled as country (And vice-versa) at somewhat alarming rates likely stems from country music’s roots in African American folk and blues music traditions that emphasize guitar driven storytelling alongside emotional themes of heartbreak, struggle, and life. With the raw and emotional delivery that they both have as a result of the early Black spiritual origins for each genre, it is completely understandable to see how the model could’ve been confused. Shovel & Rope’s blues song “The Wire” being misclassified as country is a prime example of this, with lyrical thematics centering around troubling life experiences that the American folk duo struggles with.

5. Rock ←→ Blues

Rock songs are misclassified as blues (And vice-versa) at a rather consistent scale because rock & roll as a genre actually evolved from blues in the 1950s, since numerous artists began to take inspiration from their predecessors. From blues cover songs to fully derived note patterns and progressions, the call and response vocals in both genres deal with lyrical themes that overlap in many different ways (Rebellion, relationships, hardship, good times, etc.). The model’s confusion reflects musical reality that leaves the boundary between blues music and rock music quite blurry, since both genres have roots in Black American culture. At times, there could even be a fusion of the genres to create a hybrid sub-genre called blues-rock. Without this historical context, the model assumes blues songs like Eric Clapton’s “Watch Yourself” are rock songs.

The code presented here opens up with a gradient boosting classifier to go along with the random forest classification from earlier, providing a more detailed ensemble learning technique that combines the predictions of many weak learners (shallow decision trees) to create a stronger predictive model. Unlike random forests, which trains trees independently and in parallel, gradient boosting trains trees sequentially, with each new tree correcting the errors made by the previous ones. In utilizing this model, I hoped to tackle this complex multi-classification problem where class boundaries overlap (music genres often overlap, creating sub-genres). After specifying the number of boosting stage decision trees alongside, I was effectively allowing the model to learn more complex patterns in the data, which was important for the high-dimensional audio and lyrical features present (many elements that could confuse the model). The learning rate of 0.05 meant that each individual tree held this amount of influence on the final prediction. Being smaller meant that it would slow down the learning process, making the tree contribution more conservative than before. This was done to reduce overfitting possibilities and improve generalization of the model to future scenarios in which there would be a higher number of estimators (balancing model complexity with stability). At a max depth of 3, the decision trees were shallow weak learners intentionally used in gradient boosting to prevent the memorization of training data. Now, the model could focus on broad patterns rather than individual noise, improving the ability to generalize to unseen songs on the outer portions of the dataset (outliers). The detailed curation of these parameters aided in the definition of controlled and regularized boosting processes that worked off tabular data (musical features). During the training of the model, the iteratively built decision trees were optimized over time to reduce classification errors made by the previous ones. It would soon learn how combinations of musical and lyrical features, such as danceability, energy, and valence related to specific musical genres. Once properly trained, it is utilized for the prediction of genres for the dataset with the best estimates based on learned patterns. Accuracy is assesed the same as before, with the comparisons between predicted genre labels and true genre labels in the test set being made quickly. At 42%, the level of correctness in this model has barely gotten much better since the adaptation of the random forest model. The proportion of correctly classified songs in the test data is printed alongside the precision, recall, f1-score, and support metrics from before.

  • Precision: The proportion of songs predicted as a given genre that truly belong to that genre.
  • Recall: The proportion of songs belonging to a genre that were correctly identified by the model.
  • F1-score: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, providing a balanced performance metric.
  • Support: The number of test samples for each genre.

This detailed breakdown is especially important in music genre classification, where certain genres may overlap in characteristics and be more difficult to distinguish than others. When it came to the actual values, the trends were essentially the same as before, with songs in the hip hop genre being correctly predicted as hip hop 51% of the time. This was able to happen even though only 49% of hip hop songs were initially found in the data, suggesting that hip hop’s audio and lyrical features are more distinctive in the dataset for various reasons. The continued confusion between jazz and blues or rock and pop aligns with known genre hybrids in real-world music, reinforcing the idea that some classification errors stem from genuine genre overlap rather than the model’s failure (As this model didn’t noticeably perform much “better” than the random forest model).

The incorporation of this gradient boositng alongside random forrests allows this analysis to become more error-focused and sequentially able to learn as it goes. The concentration on difficult to classify songs provides insights into genre ambiguity, leading to improved performance for complex overlapping genre classes (predictions change slightly). Furthermore, it’s good to have more than one perspective into the situation with the use of multiple models, as it will allow one to further assess the accuracy, validity, and reliability of the information at hand.

Limitations:

As musical genres have continued to evolve over time, the characteristics that define what music makes up what genre have become vague and complex. Genre conventions of the past are sometimes outdated, and modern tracks often cross boundaries more significantly than before. Many tracks are intentionally cross-genre, and strict labeling specifying what a song might intend to be is unrealistic. Despite this, my machine-learning model approached this multi-level classification problem in an attempt to accurately predict these genres. With just a few distinct audio features and lyrical elements from the songs, the model was not able to use tempo, key signatures, chord progressions, melodies, or harmonies from the records that might aid it in the quest for categorization. Furthermore, it lacked the historical context and timeline associated with each of these tunes whenever they came out, so the knowledge that shapes the genre choices throughout the dataset is inherently flawed. Numeric sentiment labels on a 0–1 scale are not enough to fully represent the song themes without some degree of noise being present in whatever metadata is being measured. Within this metadata, large amounts of bias is easily being introduced by the inclsuion of imbalanced data that overly populates the amount of songs in some genres like pop, while others like hip hop are left with very little. In the future, the use of a stronger model for audio classification instead of random forest and gradient boosting might help with the learning of genres on a deeper scale for prediction. In addition, more data from the rest of the feature columns not used in my own dataframe alongside Spotify’s Web API could aid in the data’s current lack of coherent balance, since it would be easier to pull an equal amount of songs from each genre and sub-genre in the future (given that they are originally classified correctly).

Introduction:

Music streaming services are constantly changing the way their listeners discover new artists through the use of machine-learning recommendation systems that curate an experience that aligns with a specific user’s taste. Whether it’s Spotify deploying a new weekly playlist or Apple Music recommending similar artists, machine-learning models must learn to understand what makes a song belong to a particular genre. In doing so, insights about what music garners the most attention can be properly generated in real-time. Here, supervised learning seeks to allow streaming services to predict a song’s genre using audio and lyrical features that are present within metadata. This process reveals the elements of the music that are important enough for mass appeal (Recommendation). I decided to apply this technique to a dataset of songs from many different decades to help determine a song’s genre using a mix of audio signal characteristics (e.g., acousticness, loudness, energy) and content-based features (e.g., romantic, obscene, sadness, dating). The finalized model utilized random forest classification due to the categorical nature of the endeavor, and it was able to achieve an accuracy of 41 % with the data that it was initially trained on. Although this was far from the ideal amount of accuracy that I sought to have, the model still uncovered valuable information about genre patterns and genre classification limitations in the current age of music.

Research Question:

How can musical genres be accurately mapped and predicted using certain audio and lyrical features for listeners to enjoy?

Stakeholders:

Music streaming platforms like Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube Music, and Amazon Music all have a need for user engagement on their platform, and this analysis would certainly help them with that. As new music keeps releasing every week and the demand for the next hit song increases, executives and marketing teams at these corporations will become more interested in improving how they recommend new artists and generate playlists automatically. This is especially true in situations where metadata for a song might be incomplete, or when different songs are grouped together by similarity. The complexity of the scenario further arises when music begins to get mislabeled or remains unlabeled after production. The current state of music has evolved into an amalgamation of many different genres and sub-genres, which makes it very easy for tracks to be uploaded without the selection of the correct genres that perfectly encapsulate their essence. Furthermore, the metadata that is used in its classification may vary across different record labels and eras in which the song came out (Inconsistent). As a result, it is very important for music directors at these companies to have a machine-learning model that has a good understanding of what makes a song a certain genre.

Decisions:

The development of a supervised model that can accurately detect the genre from song characteristics will allow music platforms to begin making choices that help their services to be more reliable for their users. Whether they are a casual or heavy music listener, this approach seeks to make the experience better for all. For instance, a service like Spotify might decide to generate audio tags for specific genres on tracks that don’t have good metadata, providing aid for those who may’ve been confused about what they were listening to. In addition, the ability of this learning model to work based on the data that it receives will help services like Apple Music improve similarity-based recommendations in the future, since the genres that are assigned to a song will be more precise. This functionality can be paired with a commitment to flagging songs whose genres appear to be mislabeled so that the listeners can actually discover songs that are more aligned with their general preferences.

Methods and Course Concepts Applied:

This project builds directly on multiple methodological frameworks covered throughout the course, successfully integrating both supervised and unsupervised learning techniques to analyze and predict music genres. I wanted to get a level of predictive accuracy that made sense for the data, potentially helping to understand why certain genres might be more difficult to distinguish based on audio and lyrical features present in my feature columns. To achieve this, methods from the supervised learning (module 6), model evaluation (module 7), and clustering (module 4) modules were applied.

The supervised learning methods made up the core of this project, as it relied on supervised classification, which trained models using genre label data. I was able to use it to learn relationships between numerical features (danceability, energy, and lyrical sentiment indicators) and categorical genre labels. The random forest classifier was used as the baseline supervised model, which built an ensemble of decision trees trained on random subsets of the data and features before aggregating the predictions through majority voting. Random forests are well-suited for tabular data and can detect nonlinear relationships between features without strong parametric assumptions. In this scenario, they provided a strong initial benchmark that allowed me to extract feature importance scores and get interpretability into musical and lyrical features that most influenced genre predictions overall. The gradient boosting classifier was meant to build on this random forest approach by utilizing the decision trees sequentially so that each new tree focused on correcting the errors made by previous trees. This method emphasizes difficult to classify observations and often performs well when class boundaries are complex or overlapping. Applying gradient boosting allowed for a comparison between different strategies and provided insight into how error-focused learning affects genre classification performances. When paired together, these supervised learning methods reflect concepts from the supervised learning module, including classification and model generalizations.

The model evaluation techniques were critical for understanding the model’s performance beyond a single accuracy metric. The project applies several evaluation techniques covered in the model evaluation module to assess how well the classifiers perform across different genres (multi-classification). Train-test splitting was utilized to split the dataset into training and testing subsets using a stratified approach to preserve the genre distribution. This ensured that evaluation results reflected performance on unseen data rather than memorized training examples. The overall accuracy was used as a high-level performance metric, measuring the proportion of correctly classified songs. Although its output was useful for quick and easy comparisons to be drawn across models, the accuracy alone does not capture genre class-specific performance. The classification reports provided a more nuanced evaluation showcasing precision, recall, F1-score, and support, which could be computed for each genre. Together, these metrics revealed whether certain genres were systematically over- or under-predicted and helped identify imbalanced or ambiguous genres. Confusion matrices helped to visualize prediction errors across genres by examining which genres were most frequently misunderstood by the models. The analysis revealed meaningful patterns such as overlap between pop, rock, and blues, aligning with real-world musical similarities. This evaluation method directly supports interpretability and error analysis.

The clustering and unsupervised learning analysis present in the project incorporates methods that explore the underlying structure of the data without relying too much on genre labels. For instance, K-Means clustering was applied to standardized feature data to group songs based solely on their audio and lyrical characteristics. The number of clusters was set equal to the number of genres, enabling a direct comparison between unsupervised clusters and known genre labels. This analysis helped determine whether genres naturally form distinct groups in feature space or exhibit significant overlap. Since K-Means is Euclidean distance-based, all features were standardized using z-score normalization to ensure that no single feature dominates the clustering process due to scale differences. In order to visualize the high-dimensional feature space, PCA was included to reduce the data to two principal components. PCA preserves the directions of greatest variance and allows for a two-dimensional visualization of song similarity (despite the original high-dimensionality of the song features). By having genre labels alongside cluster assignments on the PCA scatterplot, the analysis was able to reveal substantial genre overlap and explain why supervised models struggle with certain genre distributions (through another lens).

The integration of supervised classification, model evaluation, and unsupervised clustering in this project demonstrates how multiple course modules can be put into a cohesive outcome. The supervised models quantify predictions, evaluation metrics diagnose the model strengths and weaknesses, and clustering analysis provides structural insights into genre ambiguity. Together, these module methods reinforce the idea that music genre prediction is not a strictly separable classification task, but rather shaped by overlapping musical and lyrical characteristics.

gradientBoost_accuracy = accuracy_score(output_test, gradientBoost_predictions) # proportion of correct predictions out of all predictions 

print("\nGradient Boosting Model Accuracy:")
print(f"{gradientBoost_accuracy:.2f}")

print("\nGradient Boosting Classification Report:")
print(classification_report(output_test, gradientBoost_predictions))

The code presented here opens up with a gradient boosting classifier to go along with the random forest classification from earlier, providing a more detailed ensemble learning technique that combines the predictions of many weak learners (shallow decision trees) to create a stronger predictive model. Unlike random forests, which trains trees independently and in parallel, gradient boosting trains trees sequentially, with each new tree correcting the errors made by the previous ones. In utilizing this model, I hoped to tackle this complex multi-classification problem where class boundaries overlap (music genres often overlap, creating sub-genres). After specifying the number of boosting stage decision trees alongside, I was effectively allowing the model to learn more complex patterns in the data, which was important for the high-dimensional audio and lyrical features present (many elements that could confuse the model). The learning rate of 0.05 meant that each individual tree held this amount of influence on the final prediction. Being smaller meant that it would slow down the learning process, making the tree contribution more conservative than before. This was done to reduce overfitting possibilities and improve generalization of the model to future scenarios in which there would be a higher number of estimators (balancing model complexity with stability). At a max depth of 3, the decision trees were shallow weak learners intentionally used in gradient boosting to prevent the memorization of training data. Now, the model could focus on broad patterns rather than individual noise, improving the ability to generalize to unseen songs on the outer portions of the dataset (outliers). The detailed curation of these parameters aided in the definition of controlled and regularized boosting processes that worked off tabular data (musical features). During the training of the model, the iteratively built decision trees were optimized over time to reduce classification errors made by the previous ones. It would soon learn how combinations of musical and lyrical features, such as danceability, energy, and valence related to specific musical genres. Once properly trained, it is utilized for the prediction of genres for the dataset with the best estimates based on learned patterns. Accuracy is assesed the same as before, with the comparisons between predicted genre labels and true genre labels in the test set being made quickly. At 42%, the level of correctness in this model has barely gotten much better since the adaptation of the random forest model. The proportion of correctly classified songs in the test data is printed alongside the precision, recall, f1-score, and support metrics from before.

  • Precision: The proportion of songs predicted as a given genre that truly belong to that genre.
  • Recall: The proportion of songs belonging to a genre that were correctly identified by the model.
  • F1-score: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, providing a balanced performance metric.
  • Support: The number of test samples for each genre.

This detailed breakdown is especially important in music genre classification, where certain genres may overlap in characteristics and be more difficult to distinguish than others. When it came to the actual values, the trends were essentially the same as before, with songs in the hip hop genre being correctly predicted as hip hop 51% of the time. This was able to happen even though only 49% of hip hop songs were initially found in the data, suggesting that hip hop’s audio and lyrical features are more distinctive in the dataset for various reasons. The continued confusion between jazz and blues or rock and pop aligns with known genre hybrids in real-world music, reinforcing the idea that some classification errors stem from genuine genre overlap rather than the model’s failure (As this model didn’t noticeably perform much “better” than the random forest model).

The incorporation of this gradient boositng alongside random forrests allows this analysis to become more error-focused and sequentially able to learn as it goes. The concentration on difficult to classify songs provides insights into genre ambiguity, leading to improved performance for complex overlapping genre classes (predictions change slightly). Furthermore, it’s good to have more than one perspective into the situation with the use of multiple models, as it will allow one to further assess the accuracy, validity, and reliability of the information at hand.

This code assists in the creation of another confusion matrix heatmap that isolates correct prediction scores numerically on the matrix diagonal, and incorrect error prediction values for any numbers that reside off this same diagonal. Like before, each row corresponds to an actual (true) genre, and each column corresponds to a predicted genre, before placing the number of songs that fall into the cells for wherever each of them overlaps (combinations). Even though the gradient boosting model was utilized this time for the creation of this matrix, pop and country were still the most correctly predicted genres out of the 7 that were present. By this same token, the genres on the diagonal were still strong, and the systematic confusion between blues, rock, pop, and country pairs remained (attributed to shared instrumentation, thematics, and energy levels). Hip hop still has relatively fewer misclassifications, but this is because of class imbalance from the smaller group of 181 samples that it has (pop and country have over 1000 used).

Here, I developed code for clustering analysis to predict genre labels directly, as clustering provides a perspective on the data that one might not initially recognize prior to it’s incorporation. The goal of this analysis was to determine whether songs group together naturally based on their audio and lyrical features even when genre labels are not used during learning. If the clusters aligned closely with genres, then this suggested that genres were well-separated in feature space. On the other hand, substantial overlap indicates intrinsic genre ambiguity. In normalizing features before clustering, I was able to keep everything on the same scale in case any outliers made it through the previous standardization process in the original dataset. This would be essential in preventing features with larger numeric ranges from dominating the output. Now all feature columns would have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1 for K-means (distance-based algorithm with Euclidean distances). The fixed number of clusters utilized for this analysis was set equal to the number of major genres in the dataset (7), allowing for direct comparisons between learned clusters and known genre labels in the future even though genre information was not being used during clustering. After fitting the K-Means model to the standardized feature space, each song would be assigned to the nearest cluster centroid from 0 to 6 (7 total). Principal Component Analysis was needed because the feature space contained many dimensions (columns), making direct visualization imposssible. The high-dimensional data could be transformed into a two-demnsional space while preserving as much variance as possible. The first principal component represents the direction of maximum variance, while the second principal component is the second most informative direction (weighted combinations of all original variables). Upon being stored in the dataframe, they are visualized within a scatterplot that reflects each song’s overall feature profile. Color represents the genre label, and the marker style represents the cluster assignments. The algorithmically discovered clusters can be directly compared to the labeled genres, allowing one to see how each genre is forming broad overlapping regions rather than cleanly separated groups. Certain genres like pop, rock, jazz, and the blues overlap and bridge in certain areas, suggesting the shared audio and lyrical characteristics (as we might expect by this point). Regardless, the clusters present still aren’t mapping one-to-one with genres, reinforcing the idea that genre classification is inherently ambigious and hard to define clearly. The localized density regions reveal sub-genres and similarities that go across the traditional genre labels that we all know to be true. The outcome of this clustered visual provides a reasonably structured explanation for why supervised models struggle with certain genre distinctions.

In the cluster-genre distribution table, most clusters contained multiple genres rather than being dominated by a single genre, and some clusters had strong associations with particular genres despite not being exclusive to one. For example, cluster 2 had a high rock count while cluster 5 had a high country count. Hip hop was more concentrated in fewer clusters besides cluster 4, suggesting more distinctive feature patterns that didn’t allow it to fit in or experience overlap with other genres (less likely to be misidentified, lines up with higher precision values in models). The dispersion of blues, jazz, rock, and pop across many clusters highlights their stylistic commonalities.

Limitations:

As musical genres have continued to evolve over time, the characteristics that define what music makes up what genre have become vague and complex. Genre conventions of the past are sometimes outdated, and modern tracks often cross boundaries more significantly than before. Many tracks are intentionally cross-genre, and strict labeling specifying what a song might intend to be is unrealistic. Despite this, my machine-learning model approached this multi-level classification problem in an attempt to accurately predict these genres. With just a few distinct audio features and lyrical elements from the songs, the model was not able to use tempo, key signatures, chord progressions, melodies, or harmonies from the records that might aid it in the quest for categorization. Furthermore, it lacked the historical context and timeline associated with each of these tunes whenever they came out, so the knowledge that shapes the genre choices throughout the dataset is inherently flawed. Numeric sentiment labels on a 0–1 scale are not enough to fully represent the song themes without some degree of noise being present in whatever metadata is being measured. Within this metadata, large amounts of bias is easily being introduced by the inclsuion of imbalanced data that overly populates the amount of songs in some genres like pop, while others like hip hop are left with very little. In the future, the use of a stronger model for audio classification instead of random forest and gradient boosting might help with the learning of genres on a deeper scale for prediction. In addition, more data from the rest of the feature columns not used in my own dataframe alongside Spotify’s Web API could aid in the data’s current lack of coherent balance, since it would be easier to pull an equal amount of songs from each genre and sub-genre in the future (given that they are originally classified correctly).
