Predicting Music Genres with Supervised Learning: What Audio and Lyrical Features Reveal About Songs

Introduction:

Music streaming services are constantly changing the way their listeners discover new artists through the use of machine-learning recommendation systems that curate an experience that aligns with a specific user’s taste. Whether it’s Spotify deploying a new weekly playlist or Apple Music recommending similar artists, machine-learning models must learn to understand what makes a song belong to a particular genre. In doing so, insights about what music garners the most attention can be properly generated in real-time. Here, supervised learning seeks to allow streaming services to predict a song’s genre using audio and lyrical features that are present within metadata. This process reveals the elements of the music that are important enough for mass appeal (Recommendation). I decided to apply this technique to a dataset of songs from many different decades to help determine a song’s genre using a mix of audio signal characteristics (e.g., acousticness, loudness, energy) and content-based features (e.g., romantic, obscene, sadness, dating). The finalized model utilized random forest classification due to the categorical nature of the endeavor, and it was able to achieve an accuracy of 41 % with the data that it was initially trained on. Although this was far from the ideal amount of accuracy that I sought to have, the model still uncovered valuable information about genre patterns and genre classification limitations in the current age of music.

Research Question:

How can musical genres be accurately mapped and predicted using certain audio and lyrical features for listeners to enjoy?

Stakeholders:

Music streaming platforms like Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube Music, and Amazon Music all have a need for user engagement on their platform, and this analysis would certainly help them with that. As new music keeps releasing every week and the demand for the next hit song increases, executives and marketing teams at these corporations will become more interested in improving how they recommend new artists and generate playlists automatically. This is especially true in situations where metadata for a song might be incomplete, or when different songs are grouped together by similarity. The complexity of the scenario further arises when music begins to get mislabeled or remains unlabeled after production. The current state of music has evolved into an amalgamation of many different genres and sub-genres, which makes it very easy for tracks to be uploaded without the selection of the correct genres that perfectly encapsulate their essence. Furthermore, the metadata that is used in its classification may vary across different record labels and eras in which the song came out (Inconsistent). As a result, it is very important for music directors at these companies to have a machine-learning model that has a good understanding of what makes a song a certain genre.

Decisions:

The development of a supervised model that can accurately detect the genre from song characteristics will allow music platforms to begin making choices that help their services to be more reliable for their users. Whether it is a casual or heavy music listener, this approach seeks to make the experience better for all. For instance, a service like Spotify might decide to generate audio tags for specific genres on tracks that don’t have good metadata, providing aid for those who may’ve been confused about what they were listening to. In addition, the ability of this learning model to work based on the data that it receives will help services like Apple Music improve similarity-based recommendations in the future, since the genres that are assigned to a song will be more precise. This functionality can be paired with a commitment to flagging songs whose genres appear to be mislabeled so that the listeners can actually discover songs that are more aligned with their general preferences.

Data:

This data was pulled from Kaggle, and it contains lyrics and metadata for songs that were obtained through APIs. According to the NIAID Data Discovery Portal, “the audio data was scraped using Echo Nest® API integrated engine with spotipy Python’s package. The spotipy API permits the user to search for specific genres, artists, songs, release date, etc. To obtain the lyrics we used the Lyrics Genius® API as baseURL for requesting data based on the song title and artist name”. Furthermore, the lyrical themes have been processed to display scores on themes from 0 to 1, and then are manipulated by me for a deeper picture to be unveiled in the supervised learning. With 28,372 rows and 31 columns, it represents song lyrical content labels (thematic intensity) and audio features (numeric) from multiple decades (1950–2019).

The fields are as follows:

artist_name (5,426 unique values, 28,372 total): The name of the artist or group who performed the song (STRING).

track_name (23,689 unique values, 28,372 total): The name of the song (STRING).

release_date (1950–2019, 28,372 total values): The year the song was released (INTEGER).

genre (7 unique values, 28,372 total): The musical genre category for the song (STRING).

lyrics (28,372 unique values): The raw text of the song’s lyrics (STRING).

len (28,372 unique values): The number of words in the lyrics (INTEGER).

dating (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to the themes of romance, courtship, and relationships (FLOAT).

violence (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of aggression, conflict, and physical force (FLOAT).

world/life (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of society, existence, and philosophical thought (FLOAT).

night/time (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of nighttime, the passage of time, and moments (FLOAT).

shake the audience (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of impact, excitement, and energizing the listener (FLOAT).

family/gospel (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of family, spirituality, and religion (FLOAT).

romantic (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of love, passion, and intimacy (FLOAT).

communication (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of talking, expression, and dialogue (FLOAT).

obscene (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of profanity, vulgarity, and explicit content (FLOAT).

music (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to meta-themes about music itself, instruments, or sound (FLOAT).

movement/places (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of travel, location, and motion (FLOAT).

light/visual perceptions (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of sight, illumination, and imagery (FLOAT).

family/spiritual (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of kinship and faith (FLOAT).

like/girls (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of attraction, liking, and often, specifically, women (FLOAT).

sadness (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of sorrow, heartbreak, and melancholy (FLOAT).

feelings (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of emotions, sensitivity, and affect (FLOAT).

danceability (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of dancing, rhythm, and movement (FLOAT).

loudness (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1. Likely derived from lyrics referencing volume, noise, or intensity (FLOAT).

acousticness (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1. Likely derived from lyrics referencing organic, non-electric, or soft sounds (FLOAT).

instrumentalness (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1. Likely derived from lyrics referencing instruments or music without words (FLOAT).

valence (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s positiveness. High valence sounds more positive (e.g., happy, cheerful, euphoric), while low valence sounds more negative (FLOAT).

energy (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s intensity and activity. High energy feels fast, loud, and noisy (FLOAT).

topic (28,372 unique values): A categorical label assigning the song’s main theme based on the highest scoring theme field (STRING).

age (28,372 unique values): A normalized score (0–1) representing the release date, where 1.0 is the oldest (1950), and 0.0 is the newest (2019) in the dataset (FLOAT).

To predict genre, two categories of feature columns were relied upon:

  1. Audio features (numeric, continuous):
  • Danceability
  • Loudness
  • Acousticness
  • Instrumentalness
  • Energy
  • Valence

These relate to the “feel” of a song and are modeled after Spotify’s audio features.

2. Lyrical sentiment/context Features (numeric, continuous):

  • Romantic
  • Violence
  • Obscene
  • Dating
  • Sadness

These reflect language usage in lyrics and attempt to quantify emotional or thematic content.

Ground-Truth Labels:

The supervised labels from the dataset’s genre field, with some represented better than others:

  • Pop
  • Rock
  • Jazz
  • Hip hop
  • Country
  • Reggae
  • Blues

These labels serve as the supervised ground truth, assigned based on metadata sources from music databases and catalog labels.

Exploratory Data Analysis (Supervised Learning):

Conducted in a Python Jupyter Notebook environment using pandas, numpy, sklearn, matplotlib, and seaborn.

The need to categorize genres based on the given information from the dataset called for the utilization of a multi-classification supervised learning environment, as genre is a categorical variable (hip hop, jazz, reggae, etc.). With 7 possible classes, the data was non-numeric, and regression would in no way be appropriate.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, confusion_matrix, accuracy_score
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# data loaded

df = pd.read_csv('tcc_ceds_music.csv')


print(f"Shape of Data: {df.shape}") # rows/columns

# missing values check 
print("Missing values:")
print(df[['genre', 'danceability', 'energy', 'valence']].isnull().sum()) # counting and summing up empty/missing areas

# genres for classification
major_genres = ['pop', 'rock', 'jazz', 'hip hop', 'country', 'reggae', 'blues']
df_2 = df[df['genre'].isin(major_genres)].copy() # new data frame to manipulate 

# features used to predict genre of a song
feature_columns = ['danceability', 'loudness', 'acousticness', 'instrumentalness', 
                  'valence', 'energy', 'dating', 'violence', 'romantic', 'obscene', 'sadness']

input = df_2[feature_columns] # storing features for input that the model can learn from 
output = df_2['genre'] # target labeling info that the model must predict 

# splitting the data for 80/20 train/test compilation
input_train, input_test, output_train, output_test = train_test_split(input, output, test_size=0.2, stratify=output)

# training model
rf_model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100)
rf_model.fit(input_train, output_train) # fit the random forest model to the training data so that it can learn patterns

This code showcases my initial approach to this multi-classification problem after loading the data and confirming that there were no missing values, then creating a new data frame that contained all the genres I wanted to examine. After creating this copy, I selected 11 total features that would help my model learn numeric patterns from the 0–1 scale that was given to measure them. By blending audio characteristics and lyrical sentiment, I could see a balanced picture that conceptually tied into the genre. For example, Jazz tends to have high instrumentalness throughout the record, while hip hop delves into high obscenity or violence scores. On the other hand, pop tends to be high in danceability and valence, while the blues are high in sadness and romance. After defining the features that the model was to learn from, I specified what it was supposed to be predicting (genres) so that the data could be split into an 80% training set and a 20% testing set that stratified the result by genre. In doing this, I could preserve a distribution that best represented the entire population in an unbiased and generalizable way despite the imbalanced data that had a large number of songs in some genres but not others (e.g., 7042 songs vs 904 hip hop songs). I used a random forest classification model since the genre-feature relationship I was creating worked with non-linear connections. This would also mean that noise and irrelevant variables could be handled better before the production of feature importance metrics that are critical for creating insights. The random forest model performs well with mixed-scale numeric variables, so no feature standardization was required. Even though this dataset had 7 genres whose features could vary at any given point in time, the use of multiple decision trees (100) circumvented this issue well.

Classification Report:

# predict genre
output_prediction = rf_model.predict(input_test) # begins predicting genre for input set of feature columns 

# accuracy score
accuracy = accuracy_score(output_test, output_prediction) # compares predictions for genre with what genre labels for each song actually were 
print(f"Model Accuracy: {accuracy:.2f}")
print("Classification Report:")
print(classification_report(output_test, output_prediction)) # showcasing performance metrics for each genre analyzed

"""
Precision: How many predicted as X were actually X (Reliability)
Recall: How many actual X were correctly predicted as X (Validity)
F1-Score: Balance between precision and recall
Support: Number of samples for each genre 
"""

Model Accuracy: 0.41
Classification Report:
              precision    recall  f1-score   support

       blues       0.35      0.30      0.32       921
     country       0.42      0.54      0.47      1089
     hip hop       0.55      0.43      0.48       181
        jazz       0.48      0.37      0.42       769
         pop       0.37      0.43      0.40      1408
      reggae       0.48      0.47      0.48       500
        rock       0.44      0.33      0.37       807

    accuracy                           0.41      5675
   macro avg       0.44      0.41      0.42      5675
weighted avg       0.42      0.41      0.41      5675

This code block reveals how genres were predicted from the input of each feature column before the assignment of an accuracy score and a classification report. The accuracy rating of 41% was lower than expected, but it still made sense for the given data that had 7 genres with many overlapping characteristics that could easily be misinterpreted by the model. It’s also likely that the lower rating was exacerbated by the sheer amount of imbalance in data representation that existed among the genres. This could easily happen despite my best efforts to contain it. Regardless, the model fares 3 times better than the base chance one would have off simply predicting what genre the song is using observations alone, since the ratio for that scenario would be 1/7 (yielding a 14% chance of guessing right on each attempt). The classification report told a vivid story about how each genre actually performed in the model, utilizing precision, recall, f1-score, and support as measurements. Precision represents the percentage metric that shows songs predicted as genre X that actually were genre X, while recall takes the songs that actually were genre X and displays what percentage were correctly predicted (Ratio flipped). The f1-score extracts the harmonic mean of precision and recall together to showcase the balance that exists between them. Support simply represented the number of samples being used for each of these genres. Genres like hip-hop performed quite well, with a precision score of 0.55 and a recall score of 0.43. This meant that whenever the model predicted that a song was hip hop, it was right 55% of the time and found 43% of hip hop songs in total, as hip hop has distinctive features that make it a bit easier to identify. Genres like the blues did poorly with a precision score of 0.35 and a recall score of 0.30, meaning that 70% of blues records were missed and only 35% of actual predictions were correct within the 30% that were analyzed. However, this makes sense, since blues as a genre is often emulated and used as inspiration for the creation of music in many other genres that are present in the dataset. As a result, it is quite easy for the model to miss out on certain portions of the musical landscape that are heavily influenced by soulful music (Share a lot of similar audio features).

Plot 1:

# confusion matrix heatmap to display correct and incorrect predictions 
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 8))
heatmap_cm = confusion_matrix(output_test, output_prediction) # predictions on the diagonal are correct, but predictions off of the diagonal are incorrect errors
sns.heatmap(heatmap_cm, annot=True, fmt='d', cmap='YlOrRd', # display numbers as integers (no floating point values) with color scheming
            xticklabels=rf_model.classes_, 
            yticklabels=rf_model.classes_) # tick mark labeling corresponding to genres (classes)
plt.title('Genre Classification Confusion Matrix')
plt.xlabel('Predicted Genre')
plt.ylabel('True Genre')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

This code assists in generating a confusion matrix heatmap that isolates correct prediction scores numerically on the matrix diagonal, and incorrect error prediction values for any numbers that reside off the diagonal. In providing valid labeling for each tick mark, it becomes clear to see that pop and country were the most correctly predicted genres out of the 7 that were present. Most genres on the diagonal were about in the middle for prediction accuracy, with hip hop being the only outlier due to class imbalance (Hip hop only has 181 samples, while pop and country have over 1000), and genre ambiguity issues (Feature overlap). Hints of genre misclassifications existed between the pop-country pairs, pop-rock pairs, blues-country pairs, and blues-pop pairs. However, this is likely due to the lack of granularity and genre distinctions for audios that are sonically similar to one another. 2. Rock → Pop

Rock songs being predicted as pop were common misclassifications due to the soft, melodic, or acoustic sounds from rock music that can often strcturally resemble pop music on many different levels. From varying levels of volume and energy to high amounts of valence, the room for mistakes with a machine-learning model that can’t necessairly distinguish actual sounds in the music is high. U2’s rock song “God Part II” was incorrectly assesed as a pop song due to it’s high level of valence and energy that one could also dance to, while Imagine Dragons’ rock song “Yesterday” was predicted to be pop music because it was well-rounded in these same areas.

3. Blues ←→ Pop

Blues songs being predicted as pop (And vice-versa) happened at a suprisingly high rate due to the level of influence blues has as a genre that the machine-learning model isn’t able to distinguish without historical context. Pop music as a whole evolved and countinues to develop from blues/r&b roots with many similar chord progressions. Emotional and soulful singing often appears in both as a result of this reality, with singers like Adele being placed in the pop genre despite their sound being curated by traditional Black blues artists. Blues songs like The animals’ “Many Rivers to Cross” and Joe Cocker’s “I Stand in Wonder” were incorrectly predicted as pop songs for this exact reason. As perfect examples of this occurrence, “Many Rivers to Cross” is originally a song that comes from the Black reggae artist Jimmy Cliff, and Joe Cocker was heavily influenced by the soulful music Black Americans made in the 60s and 70s.

4. Blues ←→ Country

Blues songs being incorrectly labeled as country (And vice-versa) at somewhat alarming rates likely stems from country music’s roots in African American folk and blues music traditions that emphasizes guitar driven story telling alongside emotional themes of heartbreak, struggle, and life. With the raw and emotional delivery that they both have as a result of the early Black spiritual origins for each genre, it is completely understandable to see how the model could’ve been confused. Shovel & Rope’s blues song “The Wire” being misclassified as country is a prime example of this, with lyrical thematics centering around troubling life experiences that the American folk duo struggles with.

5. Rock ←→ Blues

Rock songs aremisclassified as blues (And vice-versa) at a rather consistent scale because rock & roll as a genre actually evolved from blues in the 1950s, since numerous artists began to take inspiration from their predecessors. From blues cover songs to fully derived note patterns and progressions, the call and response vocals in both genres deal with lyrical themes that overlap in many different ways (Rebellion, relationships, hardship, good times, etc.). The model’s confusion reflects musical reality that leaves the boundary between blues music and rock music quite blurry, since both genres have roots in Black American culture. At times, there could even be a fusion of the genres to create a hybrid sub-genre called blues-rock. Without this historical context, the model assumes blues songs like Eric Clapton’s “Watch Yourself” are rock songs.

Predicting Music Genres with Supervised Learning: What Audio and Lyrical Features Reveal About Songs

Introduction:

Music streaming services are constantly changing the way their listeners discover new artists through the use of machine-learning recommendation systems that curate an experience that aligns with a specific user’s taste. Whether it’s Spotify deploying a new weekly playlist or Apple Music recommending similar artists, machine-learning models must learn to understand what makes a song belong to a particular genre. In doing so, insights about what music garners the most attention can be properly generated in real-time. Here, supervised learning seeks to allow streaming services to predict a song’s genre using audio and lyrical features that are present within metadata. This process reveals the elements of the music that are important enough for mass appeal (Recommendation). I decided to apply this technique to a dataset of songs from many different decades to help determine a song’s genre using a mix of audio signal characteristics (e.g., acousticness, loudness, energy) and content-based features (e.g., romantic, obscene, sadness, dating). The finalized model utilized random forest classification due to the categorical nature of the endeavor, and it was able to achieve an accuracy of 41 % with the data that it was initially trained on. Although this was far from the ideal amount of accuracy that I sought to have, the model still uncovered valuable information about genre patterns and genre classification limitations in the current age of music.

Research Question:

How can musical genres be accurately mapped and predicted using certain audio and lyrical features for listeners to enjoy?

Stakeholders:

Music streaming platforms like Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube Music, and Amazon Music all have a need for user engagement on their platform, and this analysis would certainly help them with that. As new music keeps releasing every week and the demand for the next hit song increases, executives and marketing teams at these corporations will become more interested in improving how they recommend new artists and generate playlists automatically. This is especially true in situations where metadata for a song might be incomplete, or when different songs are grouped together by similarity. The complexity of the scenario further arises when music begins to get mislabeled or remains unlabeled after production. The current state of music has evolved into an amalgamation of many different genres and sub-genres, which makes it very easy for tracks to be uploaded without the selection of the correct genres that perfectly encapsulate their essence. Furthermore, the metadata that is used in its classification may vary across different record labels and eras in which the song came out (Inconsistent). As a result, it is very important for music directors at these companies to have a machine-learning model that has a good understanding of what makes a song a certain genre.

Decisions:

The development of a supervised model that can accurately detect the genre from song characteristics will allow music platforms to begin making choices that help their services to be more reliable for their users. Whether it is a casual or heavy music listener, this approach seeks to make the experience better for all. For instance, a service like Spotify might decide to generate audio tags for specific genres on tracks that don’t have good metadata, providing aid for those who may’ve been confused about what they were listening to. In addition, the ability of this learning model to work based on the data that it receives will help services like Apple Music improve similarity-based recommendations in the future, since the genres that are assigned to a song will be more precise. This functionality can be paired with a commitment to flagging songs whose genres appear to be mislabeled so that the listeners can actually discover songs that are more aligned with their general preferences.

Data:

This data was pulled from Kaggle, and it contains lyrics and metadata for songs that were obtained through APIs. According to the NIAID Data Discovery Portal, “the audio data was scraped using Echo Nest® API integrated engine with spotipy Python’s package. The spotipy API permits the user to search for specific genres, artists, songs, release date, etc. To obtain the lyrics we used the Lyrics Genius® API as baseURL for requesting data based on the song title and artist name”. Furthermore, the lyrical themes have been processed to display scores on themes from 0 to 1, and then are manipulated by me for a deeper picture to be unveiled in the supervised learning. With 28,372 rows and 31 columns, it represents song lyrical content labels (thematic intensity) and audio features (numeric) from multiple decades (1950–2019).

The fields are as follows:

artist_name (5,426 unique values, 28,372 total): The name of the artist or group who performed the song (STRING).

track_name (23,689 unique values, 28,372 total): The name of the song (STRING).

release_date (1950–2019, 28,372 total values): The year the song was released (INTEGER).

genre (7 unique values, 28,372 total): The musical genre category for the song (STRING).

lyrics (28,372 unique values): The raw text of the song’s lyrics (STRING).

len (28,372 unique values): The number of words in the lyrics (INTEGER).

dating (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to the themes of romance, courtship, and relationships (FLOAT).

violence (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of aggression, conflict, and physical force (FLOAT).

world/life (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of society, existence, and philosophical thought (FLOAT).

night/time (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of nighttime, the passage of time, and moments (FLOAT).

shake the audience (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of impact, excitement, and energizing the listener (FLOAT).

family/gospel (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of family, spirituality, and religion (FLOAT).

romantic (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of love, passion, and intimacy (FLOAT).

communication (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of talking, expression, and dialogue (FLOAT).

obscene (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of profanity, vulgarity, and explicit content (FLOAT).

music (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to meta-themes about music itself, instruments, or sound (FLOAT).

movement/places (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of travel, location, and motion (FLOAT).

light/visual perceptions (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of sight, illumination, and imagery (FLOAT).

family/spiritual (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of kinship and faith (FLOAT).

like/girls (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of attraction, liking, and often, specifically, women (FLOAT).

sadness (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of sorrow, heartbreak, and melancholy (FLOAT).

feelings (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of emotions, sensitivity, and affect (FLOAT).

danceability (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s relevance to themes of dancing, rhythm, and movement (FLOAT).

loudness (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1. Likely derived from lyrics referencing volume, noise, or intensity (FLOAT).

acousticness (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1. Likely derived from lyrics referencing organic, non-electric, or soft sounds (FLOAT).

instrumentalness (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1. Likely derived from lyrics referencing instruments or music without words (FLOAT).

valence (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s positiveness. High valence sounds more positive (e.g., happy, cheerful, euphoric), while low valence sounds more negative (FLOAT).

energy (28,372 unique values): A score from 0 to 1 indicating the lyrical content’s intensity and activity. High energy feels fast, loud, and noisy (FLOAT).

topic (28,372 unique values): A categorical label assigning the song’s main theme based on the highest scoring theme field (STRING).

age (28,372 unique values): A normalized score (0–1) representing the release date, where 1.0 is the oldest (1950), and 0.0 is the newest (2019) in the dataset (FLOAT).

To predict genre, two categories of feature columns were relied upon:

  1. Audio features (numeric, continuous):
  • Danceability
  • Loudness
  • Acousticness
  • Instrumentalness
  • Energy
  • Valence

These relate to the “feel” of a song and are modeled after Spotify’s audio features.

2. Lyrical sentiment/context Features (numeric, continuous):

  • Romantic
  • Violence
  • Obscene
  • Dating
  • Sadness

These reflect language usage in lyrics and attempt to quantify emotional or thematic content.

Ground-Truth Labels:

The supervised labels from the dataset’s genre field, with some represented better than others:

  • Pop
  • Rock
  • Jazz
  • Hip hop
  • Country
  • Reggae
  • Blues

These labels serve as the supervised ground truth, assigned based on metadata sources from music databases and catalog labels.

Exploratory Data Analysis (Supervised Learning):

Conducted in a Python Jupyter Notebook environment using pandas, numpy, sklearn, matplotlib, and seaborn.

The need to categorize genres based on the given information from the dataset called for the utilization of a multi-classification supervised learning environment, as genre is a categorical variable (hip hop, jazz, reggae, etc.). With 7 possible classes, the data was non-numeric, and regression would in no way be appropriate.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, confusion_matrix, accuracy_score
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# data loaded

df = pd.read_csv('tcc_ceds_music.csv')


print(f"Shape of Data: {df.shape}") # rows/columns

# missing values check 
print("Missing values:")
print(df[['genre', 'danceability', 'energy', 'valence']].isnull().sum()) # counting and summing up empty/missing areas

# genres for classification
major_genres = ['pop', 'rock', 'jazz', 'hip hop', 'country', 'reggae', 'blues']
df_2 = df[df['genre'].isin(major_genres)].copy() # new data frame to manipulate 

# features used to predict genre of a song
feature_columns = ['danceability', 'loudness', 'acousticness', 'instrumentalness', 
                  'valence', 'energy', 'dating', 'violence', 'romantic', 'obscene', 'sadness']

input = df_2[feature_columns] # storing features for input that the model can learn from 
output = df_2['genre'] # target labeling info that the model must predict 

# splitting the data for 80/20 train/test compilation
input_train, input_test, output_train, output_test = train_test_split(input, output, test_size=0.2, stratify=output)

# training model
rf_model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100)
rf_model.fit(input_train, output_train) # fit the random forest model to the training data so that it can learn patterns

This code showcases my initial approach to this multi-classification problem after loading the data and confirming that there were no missing values, then creating a new data frame that contained all the genres I wanted to examine. After creating this copy, I selected 11 total features that would help my model learn numeric patterns from the 0–1 scale that was given to measure them. By blending audio characteristics and lyrical sentiment, I could see a balanced picture that conceptually tied into the genre. For example, Jazz tends to have high instrumentalness throughout the record, while hip hop delves into high obscenity or violence scores. On the other hand, pop tends to be high in danceability and valence, while the blues are high in sadness and romance. After defining the features that the model was to learn from, I specified what it was supposed to be predicting (genres) so that the data could be split into an 80% training set and a 20% testing set that stratified the result by genre. In doing this, I could preserve a distribution that best represented the entire population in an unbiased and generalizable way despite the imbalanced data that had a large number of songs in some genres but not others (e.g., 7042 songs vs 904 hip hop songs). I used a random forest classification model since the genre-feature relationship I was creating worked with non-linear connections. This would also mean that noise and irrelevant variables could be handled better before the production of feature importance metrics that are critical for creating insights. The random forest model performs well with mixed-scale numeric variables, so no feature standardization was required. Even though this dataset had 7 genres whose features could vary at any given point in time, the use of multiple decision trees (100) circumvented this issue well.

Classification Report:

Recall: How many actual X were correctly predicted as X (Validity)
F1-Score: Balance between precision and recall

"""

This code block reveals how genres were predicted from the input of each feature column before the assignment of an accuracy score and a classification report. The accuracy rating of 41% was lower than expected, but it still made sense for the given data that had 7 genres with many overlapping characteristics that could easily be misinterpreted by the model. It’s also likely that the lower rating was exacerbated by the sheer amount of imbalance in data representation that existed among the genres. This could easily happen despite my best efforts to contain it. Regardless, the model fares 3 times better than the base chance one would have off simply predicting what genre the song is using observations alone, since the ratio for that scenario would be 1/7 (yielding a 14% chance of guessing right on each attempt). The classification report told a vivid story about how each genre actually performed in the model, utilizing precision, recall, f1-score, and support as measurements. Precision represents the percentage metric that shows songs predicted as genre X that actually were genre X, while recall takes the songs that actually were genre X and displays what percentage were correctly predicted (Ratio flipped). The f1-score extracts the harmonic mean of precision and recall together to showcase the balance that exists between them. Support simply represented the number of samples being used for each of these genres. Genres like hip-hop performed quite well, with a precision score of 0.55 and a recall score of 0.43. This meant that whenever the model predicted that a song was hip hop, it was right 55% of the time and found 43% of hip hop songs in total, as hip hop has distinctive features that make it a bit easier to identify. Genres like the blues did poorly with a precision score of 0.35 and a recall score of 0.30, meaning that 70% of blues records were missed and only 35% of actual predictions were correct within the 30% that were analyzed. However, this makes sense, since blues as a genre is often emulated and used as inspiration for the creation of music in many other genres that are present in the dataset. As a result, it is quite easy for the model to miss out on certain portions of the musical landscape that are heavily influenced by soulful music (Share a lot of similar audio features).

Most genres on the diagonal were about in the middle for prediction accuracy, with hip hop being the only outlier due to class imbalance (Hip hop only has 181 samples, while pop and country have over 1000), and genre ambiguity issues (Feature overlap). Hints of genre misclassifications existed between the pop-country pairs, pop-rock pairs, blues-country pairs, and blues-pop pairs. However, this is likely due to the lack of granularity and genre distinctions for audios that are sonically similar to one another. Regardless, the outcome of this confusion matrix is still within reason, since the borders between each genre are blurry. Musical features alone don’t strictly enforce categorical boundaries, so the presence of mistakes in some areas makes perfect sense.

Plot 2:

This code block generates a horizontal bar chart using a dataframe that ranks the machine-learning model’s feature importance for each attribute. After sorting the chart to hold each bar in the valid order and assigning a score of importance that is visibly distinguished by color, I was able to definitively see the values for each feature. Out of the 11 features that were present for analysis, Danceability, acousticness, energy, instrumentalness, and valence were deemed to be the top 5 most important, with scores around 0.08 model contribution or higher. This meant that each one of these features influenced 8% or more of the model’s decisions for genre prediction. Altogether, these 11 add up to account for 100% of the model’s decision-making process. The lack of prevalent scores toward the lower end of the graph likely explains why some genres don’t get accurately analyzed by the model. Sometimes this could be attributed to less support from the training data (samples). Despite all of this, the outcome is still within intuitive expectations.

  • Danceability distinguishes pop from jazz, blues, and rock
  • Acousticness helps identify folk-influenced genres like country
  • Energy separates hip hop and rock from jazz
  • Instrumentalness is critical for traditional jazz and modern instrumental jazz
  • Valence distinguishes darker-toned genres from upbeat ones

The least influential features ended up being dating, romance, sadness, obscenity, and violence, indicating that lyrical content contributes to genre predictions less than audio features. This sort of information is extremely valuable in the development of recommendation systems for said music throughout various streaming services.

Misclassifications:

This code block showcases my approach to listing a few songs that were misclassified alongside the patterns that emerged from their misclassification on a broad scale. In linking the indices of the test set of data for the model back to the original data that held the song information, I was able to create and merge a data frame full of the model’s genre prediction results with song details (provided that they were initially available/existed). From here, I noted the number of songs that were misclassified and came out with a rate of around 59%. This made sense, as the accuracy rating for the original model came out to be around 41%, allowing for the full capabilities of prediction to be verified since 100–41 = 59 (100% in total). After iterating through the top 15 misclassified songs with consistent formatting for the output, I decided to include the values of audio features that each of these distinct songs had, so that an explanation for their misclassification could be uncovered. The actual vs predicted genre frequency table (matrix) was created with this same goal in mind, and the top 5 pairs of genres that the model got confused were sorted through efficiently.

  1. Pop ←→ Country

Pop songs incorrectly labeled as country records (And vice-versa) consistently occurred as an issue in the model’s predictions, as these two genres held the highest amount of representation within the data out of the 7 present. They also crossover a lot in modern music to produce records with high acousticness, danceability, and sentimental lyrical themes. Without a reliable means of delineating instrumentation beyond the feature rating given in the data, the machine-learning model likely can’t differentiate between the two genres well enough for accuracy purposes. Pop songs like Post Malone’s “Blame It on Me” were predicted to be country due to its high danceability, energy, and lyrics, while country songs like Blake Shelton’s “Home” were predicted to be pop due to its balanced acoustic nature.

2. Rock → Pop

Rock songs being predicted as pop were common misclassifications due to the soft, melodic, or acoustic sounds from rock music that can often strcturally resemble pop music on many different levels. From varying levels of volume and energy to high amounts of valence, the room for mistakes with a machine-learning model that can’t necessairly distinguish actual sounds in the music is high. U2’s rock song “God Part II” was incorrectly assesed as a pop song due to it’s high level of valence and energy that one could also dance to, while Imagine Dragons’ rock song “Yesterday” was predicted to be pop music because it was well-rounded in these same areas.

3. Blues ←→ Pop

Blues songs being predicted as pop (And vice-versa) happened at a suprisingly high rate due to the level of influence blues has as a genre that the machine-learning model isn’t able to distinguish without historical context. Pop music as a whole evolved and countinues to develop from blues/r&b roots with many similar chord progressions. Emotional and soulful singing often appears in both as a result of this reality, with singers like Adele being placed in the pop genre despite their sound being curated by traditional Black blues artists. Blues songs like The animals’ “Many Rivers to Cross” and Joe Cocker’s “I Stand in Wonder” were incorrectly predicted as pop songs for this exact reason. As perfect examples of this occurrence, “Many Rivers to Cross” is originally a song that comes from the Black reggae artist Jimmy Cliff, and Joe Cocker was heavily influenced by the soulful music Black Americans made in the 60s and 70s.

4. Blues ←→ Country

Blues songs being incorrectly labeled as country (And vice-versa) at somewhat alarming rates likely stems from country music’s roots in African American folk and blues music traditions that emphasizes guitar driven story telling alongside emotional themes of heartbreak, struggle, and life. With the raw and emotional delivery that they both have as a result of the early Black spiritual origins for each genre, it is completely understandable to see how the model could’ve been confused. Shovel & Rope’s blues song “The Wire” being misclassified as country is a prime example of this, with lyrical thematics centering around troubling life experiences that the American folk duo struggles with.

5. Rock ←→ Blues

Rock songs aremisclassified as blues (And vice-versa) at a rather consistent scale because rock & roll as a genre actually evolved from blues in the 1950s, since numerous artists began to take inspiration from their predecessors. From blues cover songs to fully derived note patterns and progressions, the call and response vocals in both genres deal with lyrical themes that overlap in many different ways (Rebellion, relationships, hardship, good times, etc.). The model’s confusion reflects musical reality that leaves the boundary between blues music and rock music quite blurry, since both genres have roots in Black American culture. At times, there could even be a fusion of the genres to create a hybrid sub-genre called blues-rock. Without this historical context, the model assumes blues songs like Eric Clapton’s “Watch Yourself” are rock songs.

Limitations:

As musical genres have continued to evolve over time, the characteristics that define what music makes up what genre have become vague and complex. Genre conventions of the past are sometimes outdated, and modern tracks often cross boundaries more significantly than before. Many tracks are intentionally cross-genre, and strict labeling specifying what a song might intend to be is unrealistic. Despite this, my machine-learning model approached this multi-level classification problem in an attempt to accurately predict these genres. With just a few distinct audio features and lyrical elements from the songs, the model was not able to use tempo, key signatures, chord progressions, melodies, or harmonies from the records that might aid it in the quest for categorization. Furthermore, it lacked the historical context and timeline associated with each of these tunes whenever they came out, so the knowledge that shapes the genre choices throughout the dataset is inherently flawed. Numeric sentiment labels on a 0–1 scale are not enough to fully represent the song themes without some degree of noise being present in whatever metadata is being measured. Within this metadata, large amounts of bias is easily being introduced by the inclsuion of imbalanced data that overly populates the amount of songs in some genres like pop, while others like hip hop are left with very little. In the future, the use of a stronger model for audio classification instead of random forest might help with the learning of genres on a deeper scale for prediction.

items.description:
Introduction:

The digitally connected world of today has found itself in a complex and modernized ecosystem of users that build easy-to-access communities based on shared interests, behaviors, and connection patterns. This ecosystem is often navigated through the lens of social media platforms like Twitter. Whether it be a celebrity, influencer, or your average everyday user, communities are built on the user’s authenticity and willingness to engage with the platform on a deep level. The niche and convoluted spaces that develop as a result of so many internet personalities colliding with one another create a breeding ground for innovation, creativity, and noteworthy relationships that certain clustering algorithms can easily reveal. For Business owners, marketing managers, and developers on social media, understanding this information is quite important, as the nuances of online communities are crucial for making effective engagement strategies. This clustering analysis will not only reveal the structure that holds up Twitter’s social fabric for its users, but it will also provide the data-driven insights necessary for decisions in the near future.

Research Question:

What types of user communities exist within Twitter’s social network, and how can they be structurally assessed for influence?

Stakeholders:

The directors of Twitter’s social media marketing team will significantly benefit from the findings of this analysis, as they have a need to increase the level of engagement that users have with their product on a daily basis. The desire to tailor content on the network to an individual’s liking holds extreme importance for revenue and returns on investment for business owners on the platform. Without a concrete plan in mind that measures the stability of the framework that the network is currently using, it will undoubtedly fail to reach the heights that it could potentially reach. This is especially true in times of high activity, where the products that are managed and marketed on Twitter are visible to a lot of people who likely would need a reason to continue to spend their time there. When tallying up the number of individuals who undergo this process, there is a need to extrapolate the reliability of the solution for all the communities that it might affect.

Decisions:

In following through with a plan for the marketing director’s team, Twitter can begin identifying which types of communities are most relevant, while still attempting to offer benefits to the more niche types that will still be affected by their assessments. This is very important, as the goal for all businesses is to maximize profit while simultaneously minimizing costs. By offering a solution that is practical to the many groups that it might affect, you can effectively sustain everything by generating financial gains and engagement in all areas. Furthermore, by tailoring their strategies to different communities alongside budget allocation, the marketing team will be able to design community-specific campaigns that address their desires promptly.

Data:

This data was pulled from Stanford’s Large Network Dataset Collection (SNAP), and represents a Twitter Social Network Graph that uncovers a subset of Twitter users from the year 2012 (SNAP: Network Datasets: Social Circles, n.d.-b). The follower-to-followee relationships make up the network’s structure and edge list, and the fields in the file consist of a Source user ID and a target user ID. With an initial sample size of 81,306 nodes and 1,768,149 edges, it was expansive enough to encapsulate a valid relationship. However, in the interest of reliable and computationally efficient analysis times, I viewed it through a smaller sample size of 428 nodes and 7174 edges (Pulled from 10,000 edges). After loading and carefully parsing the anonymized data with Python libraries and capabilities, it was clear to see the importance of the relationships that each node may have had with one another before I even conducted clustering analysis. As a result, the processed data quickly allowed me to understand how certain influential communities are built and assessed on Twitter’s algorithms.

Nodes (STRING): 428 → Converted to INT

Edges (STRING): 7174 → Converted to INT

Exploratory Data Analysis:

Conducted in Python Jupyter Notebook environment using networkx, pandas, numpy, scikit-learn, and matplotlib.

Plot 1:

import networkx as nx
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# load data
edges = []
with open('twitter_combined.txt', 'r') as f:
    for i, line in enumerate(f):
        if i >= 1000:  # smaller sample for speed
            break
        parts = line.strip().split()
        if len(parts) == 2:
            edges.append((int(parts[0]), int(parts[1])))


G = nx.Graph() # building graph and then adding specified stored edges
G.add_edges_from(edges)

# making nodes into list to iterate through 
node_list = list(G.nodes())

# degree
degrees = np.array([G.degree(node) for node in node_list]) # counting connections for each node to determine degree

# clustering coefficient (how interconnected a node's neighbors, value between 0 and 1)
clustering_coeffs = np.array([nx.clustering(G, node) for node in node_list])

# feature matrix
features = np.column_stack([degrees, clustering_coeffs]) # matrix where rows are nodes and columns are (degree, clustering coefficent)

# normalize data
features_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(features)

# inertia for different k values
k_range = range(1, 11)
inertia = []
for k in k_range:
    kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=50, n_init=10)
    kmeans.fit(features_scaled)
    inertia.append(kmeans.inertia_)

# elbow plot
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(k_range, inertia, 'ro-', linewidth=2, markersize=8)
plt.xlabel('Number of Clusters (k)')
plt.ylabel('Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (inertia)')
plt.title('Finding Optimal Number of Clusters (k)')
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.show()

This code block uncovers how I loaded in the data and built the initial graph structure to utilize in my analysis. In enumerating line by line through the text file, I was able to identify edges and nodes that would later be put into a list for iteration. From here, this node list could get degree values (1 to many edge connections) from the two-element arrays and reveal clustering coefficients between 0 and 1 (With 0 representing no interconnection, and 1 representing full connection). Introduction:

Cities throughout the world have all been built up by civilization to be strategically placed and curated to be socioeconomic powerhouses that revitalize traditions, growth, and expansion of resources. Whether it’s been tourist attractions, new infrastructure, or a rising star, every city on the globe has operated as a geographic hub of its own. Within that, a steady degree of importance can consistently be found in where exactly they are located. Without this realization, many cities would fail to be the successful and relevant regions we know them to be today. In building markets that seek to gain prosperity in whatever field of operations they so choose, an organization may face challenges if they do not follow the specific formulas that have worked for a firm within another city. The significance that comes from identifying two cities that share fundamental characteristics proves to be very enticing for those who want to competitively sell themselves. Businesses need the ability to systematically realize what initiatives make them the most money, and that starts with where they’re located. By leveraging cosine similarity assessments, one can easily develop data-driven strategies that deal with the corporate environment.

Research Question:

What cities should be recognized as key global business hubs for expansion purposes?

Stakeholders:

Uncovering the fundamental structural similarities that exist within the market, geographic position, and urban culture of these places will only help them flourish.

Decisions:

The cities that show up as the most influentially similar to cities like New York and Chicago (Clear economic powerhouses of the U.S.) will alert the Expansion Committee about the potential for expansion in these areas. For instance, building up a secondary unit in a new location overseas that is quite similar to a city in the U.S. might call for the need to utilize a stronger talent deployment team that works around cultural adaptation and local consumer insights or supply chains. Geographic identity becomes tied to city, country, latitude, longitude, and population metrics, which have been filtered through for optimized computational efficiency during similarity analysis. In removing rows with missing values in critical numeric fields, I secured completeness. Furthermore, any cities with a negligible population value of zero would be considered too insignificant for final calculations. This meant that the 47,805 cities across 240 countries needed to be normalized with proper scaling that wouldn’t disproportionately dominate certain similarity scores. Min/Max scaling (x — min/max — min) was implemented to conduct this process by transforming all numeric features into a consistent 0–1 scale, with preservation of relative relationships within each feature during cross-feature comparisons. Then, whenever it was time to draft the function that completed the similarity assessment, I defined a layer of operations that extracted the latitude, longitude, and population components from the normalized feature vector. If the city being queried for similarity existed, the dataset would filter its similarity search results to only include cities that were in the same country as the original. This constraint allowed for the cultural and economic context of the nation as a whole to come into play when evaluating multiple places at once. In addition, the intended usage of cosine similarity over other methods of similarity assessment meant that the overall scale of the data could be ignored in exchange for an examination of the data’s shape or proportion of features (geographic position and population form a vector pointing in a similar direction). This is much different than measuring Euclidean distances in this situation and acquiring spatial information that might emphasize geographic closeness (physically near one another) more directly when it comes to similarity. Instead, the cosine similarity offers a distinguished look at the cities that are structurally similar in terms of direction in the feature space through a mix of geography (cities with similar latitude/longitude) and demographic scale (cities with similar population sizes). In looping through and listing five cities based on this information, I was able to consistently identify the top ten most similar cities to the one originally being queried with respect to the country it was in.

Plot Review:

Based on the extent of the analysis conducted throughout many different countries, the Expansion Committes throughout the world can leverage information from particularly important cities that are similar to the socioeconomic hubs that typically define these areas. For example, for the query city New York, cities like Los Angeles (0.98 cosine similarity score) and Chicago (0.95 cosine similarity score) were considered to be the two most similar cities in terms of geographic positioning and population metrics in the U.S. It is widely known that New York itself is one of the most influential cities in the world when it concerns market characteristics, global finance, and commerce, so Chicago and Los Angeles being highly similar means that they’re likely to be just as significant for these specific purposes. In following the same formula for the nations around the globe using this very same data, we see the same pattern, and could apply business expansion rollouts as needed. All of the cities that are listed to be the most similar to the original economic powerhouse query cities would be targeted for planning, effectively generating valuable revenue and comapny outlooks.

Validation:

The main benefit of data validation revealed itself through my verification of similar query cities producing logically consistent results in each country. If I put in a city like New York, and then tried to input a city like Orlando (Flordia) immediately after, the results were around the same, with major cities being represented in both of them. Similarly, if I put a lesser populated or less known city like Little Rock (Arkansas), I would see less populated and lesser known cities related to Little Rock. After assesing the data’s quality by uncovering how many cities and overall observations that it had alongside it’s eleven columns, I sought to make sure my results were reasonable and logically consistent. Cities like Miami, Houston, and Dallas all made sense as similarly placed cities paired with New York, and the socioeconomic standing of them was usually elite. Furthermore, when the compared similarity rankings were paired with actual historical expansion performance data, one could see that the cities that showed up the most in the dataset were also those that were the most targeted by expansion performances in the real world.

Limitations:

Although the three-feature analysis model that builds itself on latitude, longitude, and population as the main contributors to the proportional scores of similarity appears to be quite reliable and stable for each city I queried, there is still potential for the output to be a bit inaccurate or misrepresented for my specific research question, since the original data didn’t include certain business factors. Economic indicators (e.g., GDP, income, employment rate), infrastructure quality (e.g., Transportation), societal changes (e.g. Taxes), and cultural context (e.g., Consumer preference, shopping habits, rapid population growth) are all business-oriented things that aren’t necessarily covered in a direct way since they’re not present in the similarity assessment parameters (Or in the dataset at all). Additionally, the lack of temporal dynamics that might describe how the population has grown (Density patterns) or failed to grow alongside economic development trends and urban expansion patterns could lead to the data not capturing the current landscape of the market and monetary cycles on a real scale that promotes change. It is already highly likely that cities with lower populations in developing or disadvantaged areas will be underrepresented by data in general, and this data doesn’t offer a means to detect them properly.

items.title: Small-World Phenomenon: A Network Analysis of Facebook’s Social Architecture
items.author: Myles Sartor
items.description:
Introduction:

Social media platforms as we know them are defined by the connections that one makes along the way. Whether it’s real-life companions, colleagues, influencers, or our family, we all develop bonds with people that we keep up with and follow on a daily basis. In the realm of Facebook, this is more true than ever, as the people we friend connect us to a broader audience throughout the world. There’s a sense of importance in identifying who truly holds influence in this digital world, where there are billions of users and interactions on a global scale. When it comes to marketing products and individuals on the platform, it becomes important to not only identify who has the most friends and connections, but also who has the connections that actually shape how information flows throughout a network of people. To model this, you need reliable and relevant networks or graphs that transform complex social connections into cohesive patterns that tell a coherent story. This exploratory social network data analysis seeks to explore 4,039 Facebook users (nodes) and 88,234 friendships (edges) to see how a social landscape is maneuvered on a broad scale. Through the usage of three different network centrality measures, I managed to discover distinct types of influential users, hubs with massive amounts of connections, and bridges between communities of users that went to more well-connected people whose friendships carried disproportionate weight. Information such as this is necessary for the fostering of a better user experience on Facebook that links everyone together. It’s also quite helpful for uncovering misinformation between users, viral or unseen content they post, and engagement they drive beyond their immediate circles. In our digitally driven and technologically focused world, this analysis helps us understand how we should be thinking about our friends on social media.

Research Question:

In a social network, which individuals hold the most strategic positions for information flow and community cohesion?

Stakeholders:

The information from this analysis is quite compelling for Social Media Product Managers who have a need to push and promote specific types of content, commodities, and initiatives for Facebook as a platform. With this in mind, there is a strategic level of importance that comes with knowing the right users to partner with on the network, and how their connections within the network shape the flow of information in the community. Furthermore, in identifying who has key relationships with others and defining what that may mean, algorithms have a better chance of distributing content to the right audience, who would then push this content and product to another audience for better returns on investment and less vulnerability.

Decisions:

The level of partnerships and collaborations that Facebook product managers can strategically develop over time becomes heightened by the discovery of the archetypes of friendships that appear to be the most important on the platform. For instance, if a large number of popular individuals appear to converge together and create a hub for connections, then they can focus their deployment on production in this area and measure success accordingly. There would also be an inclination for creators in this space to work with one another to push a commodity to more clientele, driving up impressions and reach of what was initially being marketed. In addition, the optimization of one’s content feed could be navigated through the use of the model that is trained on the network connections of the individuals in this data, allowing Facebook to showcase particularly influential or recommended material more often (Even to groups that don’t particularly search for it). The plethora of connections, bridging, and influence that they might observe under different methods of centrality in this network will only help to further define budgets, resources, success metrics, and product development within the Facebook community to its full extent while minimizing risks born from a lack of knowledge about social media interactions.

Data:

This dataset was pulled from Stanford’s SNAP research group on large network data, and it contains an edge list where each line contains two anonymized user IDs representing a mutual friendship (undirected graph). The circles within the data represented friends lists, and the survey participants who provided the data make up the nodes (profiles) and ego networks. According to the SNAP: Network Datasets: Social Circles, the “Facebook data has been anonymized by replacing the Facebook-internal ids for each user with a new value. Also, while feature vectors from this dataset have been provided, the interpretation of those features has been obscured. For instance, where the original dataset may have contained a feature “political=Democratic Party”, the new data would simply contain “political=anonymized feature 1”. Thus, using the anonymized data, it is possible to determine whether two users have the same political affiliations, but not what their individual political affiliations represent”.

Nodes (STRING): 4,039 → Converted to INT

Edges (STRING): 88,234 → Converted to INT

Although the actual makeup of the data after its anonymized is quite simple, it's still extremely important due to its representation of real relationships, mutual connections, and substantial scale. Nodes are users and their profiles, and edges are the friendships that are born from these users' connections.

Exploratory Network Data Analysis:

Conducted in a Python Jupyter Notebook environment using matplotlib and networkx for visualizations.

Descriptive Statistics and Information:

import networkx as nx
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def load_facebook_data(file_path='facebook_combined.txt'): # getting data from loaded file
    edges = []

    with open(file_path, 'r') as file_connection: 
        for line in file_connection: # line by line looping
            if line.strip(): # check if line is empty after ridding it of white space
                parts = line.strip().split() # splitting line into list of strings 
                if len(parts) == 2: # if there are 2 elements because in the split list
                    edges.append((int(parts[0]), int(parts[1]))) # convert the 2 string elements into integers and add them as a tuple into the original list for edges

    return edges

# calling function to populate edges of the file 
edges = load_facebook_data('facebook_combined.txt')

# building undirected graph (facebook friend relationships go both ways) and adding edges from list of tuples 
g = nx.Graph()
g.add_edges_from(edges)

print(f"Network Info: {g.number_of_nodes()} nodes, {g.number_of_edges()} edges")
print(f"Average degree: {sum(dict(g.degree()).values()) / g.number_of_nodes():.2f}") # getting degree values from key-value dictionary of node:degree pairs computing an average


top_k = 20 # how many of the most central nodes to print

degree_centrality = nx.degree_centrality(g)
sorted_degrees = sorted(degree_centrality.items(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
print("\nTop 20 nodes by Degree Centrality:")
for node, degree in sorted_degrees[:top_k]:
    print(f"Node {node} <--> {degree:.5f} proportion (popularity)")

betweeness_centrality = nx.betweenness_centrality(g, k = 500) # setting a k value to make program run faster (cycles through many pathways)
sorted_between = sorted(betweeness_centrality.items(), key = lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)

for node, output in sorted_between[:top_k]:
    print(f"Node {node} <--> {output:.5f} proportion (bridges between groups)")

print(f"Network diameter: {nx.diameter(g)}") # most distant pair of people/nodes connected through certain amount of mutuals/friendships (steps)


# summary descriptive statistics about the degrees of the network graph

print(f"  Min degree: {min(degrees)}") # degree for node with the least amount of friends

This code block displays how I loaded the file and returned the data’s edges line by line before building an undirected graph that I could populate with said edges. Although I was given the number of nodes and edges within this Facebook data, it was important for me to make sure that I could match my own results with this outcome, so that I could create the nodes necessary for manipulation and plotting later on. I also calculated the average number of degrees for each node/user, since this corresponds to the average number of friends that I could expect to see for each user in the dataset full of edges. In printing out the top 20 central nodes within the data for three types of network centrality, I was able to define importance in a manner that wasn’t strictly one-dimensional. For example, under degree centrality, it would be a simple contest of popularity, where the raw number of friends one had would push their profile to the top of the list. It was crucial for me to measure this, as users with high amounts of popularity proportions would ultimately be able to reach the largest number of people with their content. Node 107, 1684, and 1912 appeared to be the most important profiles under this ideology. Under betweenness centrality, the scope of the analysis would shift to being about how often a user lies on the shortest path between other users. This is extremely pivotal to understanding how these users connect different communities and control the flow of information between them by acting as a bridge. In this scenario, Node 107, 1684, and 3437 were the most important profiles to study. The last method of centrality would be the eigenvector, which measures the level of influence that exists among the nodes in the data. The more well-connected a user’s friends are, the more weight their endorsements carry, as they are connected to other important users. Here, things were slightly different, with Node 1912, 2266, and 2206 being highly influential. Overall, the top three profiles under the three types of centrality were Node 107, 1684, and 1912, as they showed up the most in the distribution of the proportions. Being the most popular and holding the most bridges to connect different social circles, Node 107 identified a user who had 1,045 direct friends on the platform. It was clear that they were the main hub of connection for the Facebook community in this dataset, as they weren’t just popular, they were strategically positioned to reach everyone they could (Highest degree and betweenness centrality). Node 1684 was a user who held the second-most-direct friend connections at 792, and was in the second-best position to reach all the other users and communities that they could, functioning as another hub and bridge for the platform (Second-highest degree and betweenness centrality). Node 1912 was slightly different in that the user here held 755 friends, but an extremely high eigenvector centrality that placed them in a role of connection to other powerful users that the previous two didn’t have. Individuals they were connected to were particularly valuable due to being well-connected themselves. In this situation, the friends on Facebook take on a stance of quality being better than quantity.

Beyond the individual profiles that held different levels of importance based on the scope I viewed them through, the network itself had properties that were particularly important to note in the long run. For one, the code block also shows the number of connected components to be computed as 1, meaning there were no isolated users separated by breaks or jumps in the network (Everyone is connected in some way). In addition, we can see that the average clustering coefficient ended up being a strong positive value of 0.6055, corresponding to the community strength of the social media network. If thought of as a percent, the value could be translated to represent a 60.55% chance that two of your friends are also friends with each other, creating a tight relationship between a majority of users on Facebook (Friends are friends of friends). The network diameter of 8 that is created from the graph reaffirms the belief that people aren’t ever really that far away from one another socially (Small world), since it showcases that even the most distant pair of individuals on the platform are only ever 8 friendship connections away at most. This means that even information and content between them will travel rather quickly across the network (Remarkably fast for everyone else).

For maximum reach, a product manager will want to partner with users who embody the qualities of Node 107, as their direct access to a large audience makes them ideal for broadcasting information to many people.

For the bridging of various communities, a product manager should look to partner with users who are similar to Node 1684, as they are the main connectors that control the flow of information between different social circles that might go unnoticed otherwise.

For overall credibility, reliability, and endorsement, users who have a lot in common with Node 1912 will be able to showcase how their friendship connections are leveraged for true social hierarchies.

The three different measures of centrality provide the executives at Facebook with the tools to effectively curate their platform in a way that recognizes those of importance in many unique ways, rather than just one way.
