Introduction:

Social media platforms as we know them are defined by the connections that one makes along the way. Whether it’s real-life companions, colleagues, influencers, or our family, we all develop bonds with people that we keep up with and follow on a daily basis. In the realm of Facebook, this is more true than ever, as the people we friend connect us to a broader audience throughout the world. There’s a sense of importance in identifying who truly holds influence in this digital world, where there are billions of users and interactions on a global scale. When it comes to marketing products and individuals on the platform, it becomes important to not only identify who has the most friends and connections, but also who has the connections that actually shape how information flows throughout a network of people. To model this, you need reliable and relevant networks or graphs that transform complex social connections into cohesive patterns that tell a coherent story. This exploratory social network data analysis seeks to explore 4,039 Facebook users (nodes) and 88,234 friendships (edges) to see how a social landscape is maneuvered on a broad scale. Through the usage of three different network centrality measures, I managed to discover distinct types of influential users, hubs with massive amounts of connections, and bridges between communities of users that went to more well-connected people whose friendships carried disproportionate weight. Information such as this is necessary for the fostering of a better user experience on Facebook that links everyone together. It’s also quite helpful for uncovering misinformation between users, viral or unseen content they post, and engagement they drive beyond their immediate circles. In our digitally driven and technologically focused world, this analysis helps us understand how we should be thinking about our friends on social media.

Research Question:

In a social network, which individuals hold the most strategic positions for information flow and community cohesion?

Stakeholders:

The information from this analysis is quite compelling for Social Media Product Managers who have a need to push and promote specific types of content, commodities, and initiatives for Facebook as a platform. With this in mind, there is a strategic level of importance that comes with knowing the right users to partner with on the network, and how their connections within the network shape the flow of information in the community. Furthermore, in identifying who has key relationships with others and defining what that may mean, algorithms have a better chance of distributing content to the right audience, who would then push this content and product to another audience for better returns on investment and less vulnerability.

Decisions:

The level of partnerships and collaborations that Facebook product managers can strategically develop over time becomes heightened by the discovery of the archetypes of friendships that appear to be the most important on the platform. For instance, if a large number of popular individuals appear to converge together and create a hub for connections, then they can focus their deployment on production in this area and measure success accordingly. There would also be an inclination for creators in this space to work with one another to push a commodity to more clientele, driving up impressions and reach of what was initially being marketed. In addition, the optimization of one’s content feed could be navigated through the use of the model that is trained on the network connections of the individuals in this data, allowing Facebook to showcase particularly influential or recommended material more often (Even to groups that don’t particularly search for it). The plethora of connections, bridging, and influence that they might observe under different methods of centrality in this network will only help to further define budgets, resources, success metrics, and product development within the Facebook community to its full extent while minimizing risks born from a lack of knowledge about social media interactions.

Data:

This dataset was pulled from Stanford’s SNAP research group on large network data, and it contains an edge list where each line contains two anonymized user IDs representing a mutual friendship (undirected graph). The circles within the data represented friends lists, and the survey participants who provided the data make up the nodes (profiles) and ego networks. According to the SNAP: Network Datasets: Social Circles, the “Facebook data has been anonymized by replacing the Facebook-internal ids for each user with a new value. Also, while feature vectors from this dataset have been provided, the interpretation of those features has been obscured. For instance, where the original dataset may have contained a feature “political=Democratic Party”, the new data would simply contain “political=anonymized feature 1”. Thus, using the anonymized data, it is possible to determine whether two users have the same political affiliations, but not what their individual political affiliations represent”.

Nodes (STRING): 4,039 → Converted to INT

Edges (STRING): 88,234 → Converted to INT

Although the actual makeup of the data after its anonymized is quite simple, it's still extremely important due to its representation of real relationships, mutual connections, and substantial scale. Nodes are users and their profiles, and edges are the friendships that are born from these users' connections.

Conducted in a Python Jupyter Notebook environment using matplotlib and networkx for visualizations.

Under betweenness centrality, the scope of the analysis would shift to being about how often a user lies on the shortest path between other users. In this scenario, Node 107, 1684, and 3437 were the most important profiles to study. The last method of centrality would be the eigenvector, which measures the level of influence that exists among the nodes in the data. Here, things were slightly different, with Node 1912, 2266, and 2206 being highly influential. Overall, the top three profiles under the three types of centrality were Node 107, 1684, and 1912, as they showed up the most in the distribution of the proportions. Being the most popular and holding the most bridges to connect different social circles, Node 107 identified a user who had 1,045 direct friends on the platform. It was clear that they were the main hub of connection for the Facebook community in this dataset, as they weren’t just popular, they were strategically positioned to reach everyone they could (Highest degree and betweenness centrality). Node 1684 was a user who held the second-most-direct friend connections at 792, and was in the second-best position to reach all the other users and communities that they could, functioning as another hub and bridge for the platform (Second-highest degree and betweenness centrality). Node 1912 was slightly different in that the user here held 755 friends, but an extremely high eigenvector centrality that placed them in a role of connection to other powerful users that the previous two didn’t have. Individuals they were connected to were particularly valuable due to being well-connected themselves. In this situation, the friends on Facebook take on a stance of quality being better than quantity.

Beyond the individual profiles that held different levels of importance based on the scope I viewed them through, the network itself had properties that were particularly important to note in the long run. For one, the code block also shows the number of connected components to be computed as 1, meaning there were no isolated users separated by breaks or jumps in the network (Everyone is connected in some way). In addition, we can see that the average clustering coefficient ended up being a strong positive value of 0.6055, corresponding to the community strength of the social media network. If thought of as a percent, the value could be translated to represent a 60.55% chance that two of your friends are also friends with each other, creating a tight relationship between a majority of users on Facebook (Friends are friends of friends). The network diameter of 8 that is created from the graph reaffirms the belief that people aren’t ever really that far away from one another socially (Small world), since it showcases that even the most distant pair of individuals on the platform are only ever 8 friendship connections away at most. This means that even information and content between them will travel rather quickly across the network (Remarkably fast for everyone else).

For the bridging of various communities, a product manager should look to partner with users who are similar to Node 1684, as they are the main connectors that control the flow of information between different social circles that might go unnoticed otherwise.

For overall credibility, reliability, and endorsement, users who have a lot in common with Node 1912 will be able to showcase how their friendship connections are leveraged for true social hierarchies.

The three different measures of centrality provide the executives at Facebook with the tools to effectively curate their platform in a way that recognizes those of importance in many unique ways, rather than just one way.

Introduction:

Music tells a compelling story about the livelihood of the general population in every era in which it exists. From the lyrics to the genre, and even the feelings or emotions that certain sounds evoke in different individuals, music is a cultural blessing that we as people love to explore. As a result, it can be very important to leverage music and the catalog of popular songs that are recorded over time, so that we can see what people like and market towards that effectively. As a tale of time for each period, you get a good grasp of societal values, technological advancements in the music space, and societal movements by the decade. This exploratory data analysis seeks to discover how music has evolved from 1950 to 2019. By examining over 20,000 songs, I’ve quantified significant developments in music on a broad and intelligible scale. From an objective standpoint, the data findings reveal the decline of romance and soft tracks about love and happiness, to the rise of explicitness alongside hardcore expressions of reality when hip-hop/rap was created in the 80s. import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from wordcloud import WordCloud

# loading the data

# showcasing a barplot for the distribution of musical genres

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))

    ax.bar_label(i, fmt='%.0f', padding=2)

# defining major themes I want to see in the plots and calculating an average on a "centered" rolling basis to smooth out trend line and clear out noise (truer rise/fall)

df['decade'] = (df['release_date'] // 10) * 10

The musical landscape itself continously shifted, and dominance lied in different areas at different periods. In the 1950s you see lower counts of music to start out, but you also see what people cared about making at the time. As time went on, more genres were created and produced on a wider scale, and others maintained or lost their former glory. For instance, in the 1950s, jazz was dominant alongside the blues, which lines up with history since these genres brokeout around this time in an era previously dominated by pop songs. However, as time goes on, pop music still retains most of the fame, while country rises up and reggae music is newly put onto the scene in the 1960s. This trend stays consistent until rock blows up in the 1980s, and hip-hop starts seeing its arrival in the late 80s and early 90s before becoming extremely popular. By the time it hits present day, everything is around the same level of popularity, but pop is still very dominant in its creation.

The trends that I observed in the data perfectly aligned with pre-established musical history as we know it. For example, the rise of obscenity and violence corresponds with the popularization of hip-hop in the early 90s and rock in the 80s. Furthermore, the sheer dominance of pop music as a whole is evidence of this same authenticity. In double-checking and reading the lyrics of songs with particularly high thematic ratings in things like obscenity, energy, or sadness, I was able to confirm the accuracy of the labeling and results that I saw. Things logically made sense when songs under blues music were typically noted as sadder than others, given the genre’s historical roots and cultural understanding.

Limitations:

There is a level of bias that comes from an overwhelming representation of pop, country, blues, and rock music that might not be here if genres were either labeled more fairly or divided into sub-genres and genre-pairs that held more songs. In having this bias, certain music becomes culturally under-represented and placed into wide-spanning genres like pop. When looking at mainstream and commercially successful music, you have to be careful of doing this, as it is important to accurately represent the diverse level of musical expression that this large time period encompasses. In addition, the analysis that I do from the thematic scores (0 to 1) requires the machine learning model (algorithms) used for the classification of certain words into specific categories to be perfect. This is nearly impossible at this stage, as it will likely struggle with sarcasm, metaphors, cultural context, and slang that it wouldn’t be able to determine as “bad” or “good”, leading to misclassification into different theme categories that some songs shouldn’t be in. Not only this, but even when these analyses prove to be correct, we still cannot draw definitive conclusions from just a correlation of data that we see in the dataset. For instance, although we can observe the rise of obscenity alongside the rise of hip-hop, the data itself does not prove one caused the other, or that hip-hop incites people to be violent. The cultural, economic, and social reasons behind these trends are more complex than what these charts can really show on their own. The biggest limitation of all also happens to not matter even if the analyses seem to be correct, since sonic audio features are not present in the initial acquisition of this data and therefore aren’t applied. The conclusions are only drawn from the lyrical content of these songs, and the bigger picture about who these artists actually are is lost (Physical identity). Instrumentation, tempo, production style, and vocal delivery all bring a dimension of music that is fundamental to how it is experienced and categorized.

Validation:

The trends that I observed in the data perfectly aligned with pre-established musical history as we know it. For example, the rise of obscenity and violence corresponds with the popularization of hip-hop in the early 90s and rock in the 80s. Furthermore, the sheer dominance of pop music as a whole is evidence of this same authenticity. In double-checking and reading the lyrics of songs with particularly high thematic ratings in things like obscenity, energy, or sadness, I was able to confirm the accuracy of the labeling and results that I saw. Things logically made sense when songs under blues music were typically noted as sadder than others, given the genre’s historical roots and cultural understanding.

Limitations:

There is a level of bias that comes from an overwhelming representation of pop, country, blues, and rock music that might not be here if genres were either labeled more fairly or divided into sub-genres and genre-pairs that held more songs. In having this bias, certain music becomes culturally under-represented and placed into wide-spanning genres like pop. When looking at mainstream and commercially successful music, you have to be careful of doing this, as it is important to accurately represent the diverse level of musical expression that this large time period encompasses. In addition, the analysis that I do from the thematic scores (0 to 1) requires the machine learning model (algorithms) used for the classification of certain words into specific categories to be perfect. This is nearly impossible at this stage, as it will likely struggle with sarcasm, metaphors, cultural context, and slang that it wouldn’t be able to determine as “bad” or “good”, leading to misclassification into different theme categories that some songs shouldn’t be in. Not only this, but even when these analyses prove to be correct, we still cannot draw definitive conclusions from just a correlation of data that we see in the dataset. For instance, although we can observe the rise of obscenity alongside the rise of hip-hop, the data itself does not prove one caused the other, or that hip-hop incites people to be violent. The cultural, economic, and social reasons behind these trends are more complex than what these charts can really show on their own. The biggest limitation of all also happens to not matter even if the analyses seem to be correct, since sonic audio features are not present in the initial acquisition of this data and therefore aren’t applied. The conclusions are only drawn from the lyrical content of these songs, and the bigger picture about who these artists actually are is lost (Physical identity). Instrumentation, tempo, production style, and vocal delivery all bring a dimension of music that is fundamental to how it is experienced and categorized.
